What’s the most unprofessional thing a doctor has said to you? I was once at the doctor’s office for a routine check-up. The doctor, a woman in her late 50s, seemed to be in a particularly foul mood that day. She barely made eye contact as she scanned my chart with a discernible air of impatience. After a perfunctory examination of my vital signs, she asked me a series of rapid-fire questions about my lifestyle. I answered honestly, detailing my diet, exercise routine, sleep patterns, and the usual litany of complaints one usually has when visiting a medical professional. Her responses were perfunctory and dismissive, and she had the demeanour of someone who’d rather be anywhere else. At one point, after I mentioned I occasionally worked late nights she muttered under her breath something along the lines of “Well, maybe that’s why you're so run down”. I thought, fair enough. I am sometimes, quite often, a little run down. But, she didn't say it in a supportive, inquisitive manner. She said it in a way that communicated an idea that I was an idiot. Near the end of the check-up, I mentioned I’d been experiencing some mild but persistent back pain. She barely looked up from her notes, and with a sigh that seemed to carry the weight of the world she stated, "Back pain? Join the club. Everyone’s got back pain. Modern life, innit?" I couldn't believe she had the audacity to say that. I understand doctors are bombarded with medical issues and patient issues day in and day out, but it's their *job* to treat the person and not the ailment. It's a delicate balancing act and more often than not, a doctor's professionalism and empathy, not necessarily their medical skill or the medical equipment they use, make all the difference. I would’ve preferred a brief explanation as to what precautions I could take and some referral to physiotherapy, rather than her making a vague declaration in a dismissive fashion. As I was leaving, and after I asked her about the possibility of painkillers or massage therapy she shrugged and then told me in her same tired tone, ‘Honestly, I’d just learn to live with it if I were you.’ I was dumbfounded. I mean what was I paying her for? To tell me to just learn to live with it? It struck me as profoundly unprofessional and it made me walk away with the firm conviction she was burnt out and that I might as well have been talking to a brick wall wearing a lab coat. I never went back.

Why do women *hate* nerdy men? This is a question that has generated a lot of debate, to say the least. I'm not sure I can confidently answer why women specifically hate nerdy men, but I can address why some women might not be attracted to them. To begin with, there is no universality to attraction. What one woman finds attractive, another may not, and what one woman considers a dealbreaker another may not. But there are commonalities, and it's likely that some commonalities exist in why some women are not attracted to ‘nerdy men,’ just as there are commonalities in why some men aren't attracted to, say, women with tattoos and piercings. The word ‘nerd’ is loaded, of course. It suggests a degree of social awkwardness that can be considered a turn-off. Social skills are hugely important in forming relationships. I would suggest that if there is a general dislike for ‘nerdy men’ among a certain segment of the population, it likely stems from poor social skills and a general lack of awareness of the feelings of others. There is also the trope that nerds are too into themselves and their ‘nerdy’ obsessions. This can be a major detractor for a lot of women and not just by women but by anyone. This can be seen in movies such as *The 40 Year Old Virgin* where the protagonist is a grown man who acts like a child. He is obsessed with comic book characters and action figures and has no idea what women like or want. He doesn’t have basic communication skills because most of his communication is based on comic books, movies and video games. This kind of behavior is unattractive. Another complaint is that they are too attached to their moms, and they are perceived as being childish and unromantic. The lack of confidence, and the feeling that they are only using you. This can be a turn-off for anyone especially a woman. I have personally seen it firsthand in my own working life. One of my co-workers was a hardcore ‘nerd’ with zero social skills and zero awareness of how he presented himself. He was always going on about some movie or a comic book or the latest videogame. He could never get a second date or form a proper relationship. His lack of social awareness and self-absorption pushed women away. This isn't a dig at ‘nerdy men,’ I would argue that they just need to understand what is expected of them.

What movies have you judged just by looking at their posters? It’s a common enough occurrence; you're strolling through the cinema, or perhaps browsing online streaming services, and a poster catches your eye. Even if you have no intention of actually watching it, the poster can leave a powerful impression. I can’t recall the total number of times I’ve done it and, I wager, neither can you. The visuals, the font, the tagline, the actors, the director - all of these aspects of a movie poster coalesce to form an initial judgement, a snap decision on whether or not it's worthy of your time. The poster is, after all, the trailer's silent, often overlooked elder sibling.  There are countless examples of the poster doing the heavy lifting of attracting people to the cinema or streaming services. The poster artwork for Jaws, the infamous grinning shark beneath a frightened swimmer. The minimalist, almost abstract posters of many art-house films. The ensemble cast lined up and posing in a way to let you know who are the good guys and the bad guys. Sometimes a movie with a seemingly simple premise will have a poster that’s complex or, when considering the target audience, too convoluted as if they were trying too hard. I've skipped such movies. Too much thought and time. There’s a certain level of artistry in designing a poster, but it has to be balanced by the need to be straightforward, to make an immediate impact and appeal to a wide audience. It's a very delicate balance. And of course there is the movie poster that features some sexy actress looking doe-eyed. That I’ll look at, at least. If anything the poster gives you a sense of expectation, but can often be completely at odds with the movie itself. How many times I've been thoroughly disappointed! This is true of the movie itself but the poster serves as the initial bait.

What is the lowest probability event you have personally witnessed? I was once waiting at a bus stop in a small town in Ireland and witnessed a series of events unfold that, in retrospect, seemed almost impossibly improbable. First, a flock of pigeons descended upon the bus shelter, a common enough sight, but these weren't ordinary city pigeons. They were all pure white, immaculate, like avian ghosts. Then, from the direction of the local church, a funeral procession arrived: a horse-drawn hearse, followed by a single, mournful bagpiper. The hearse was drawn by a pair of black, impeccably groomed Friesian horses. As the horses were passing the bus stop one of the horses, for no apparent reason, let loose a tremendous fart, a sound that echoed through the quiet street. The bagpiper paused mid-note, as though momentarily unsure whether to incorporate the blast into his lament. Then, a bus – the one I was waiting for – pulled up, and the driver, a woman with bright red hair and a face etched with perpetual disapproval, leaned out of the window and shouted at the procession: "Will you feckin' move it along? Some of us have places to be!" The bagpiper, flustered, resumed his dirge, the horses and hearse slowly continued on their way. I got on the bus, still trying to make sense of the scene. The probability of all these elements converging at that exact moment, in that exact place, felt infinitesimally small. Later that day I started to think this scenario would make a good short story.

What's your take on Imane Khelif, a biologically proven male boxer, taking part in the Women's Boxing event at the Paris Olympics 2024? This is a tricky one. On the one hand, I’m inherently against the concept. A ‘biologically proven male boxer’ in the women’s boxing event? I find that to be a disgrace and an insult to all female boxers. A male boxer is a male boxer. We are talking about the Olympics, the pinnacle of human athletic achievement. This is not some sort of social experiment. It would be a travesty and utter mockery to the sport if it materialised. You can’t just waltz in and expect to compete. The point of boxing, like all similar competitions, is for athletes to compete against those of a similar physical make-up and physiological advantages, not for the purpose of some progressive, woke agenda. But on the other hand. I have to admit that I don’t know much about Imane Khelif. The sport of boxing, like many other popular sports, has had its share of controversial incidents ranging from shady refereeing to drugs allegations. The politics surrounding Olympic participation can be complex and often opaque. I would have to assume that the decision, if allowed, involves far more nuanced considerations of the rules, regulations and biological science than I have knowledge or understanding of. Are the rules of boxing so rigid? Can they be adapted? The issue is how do you ascertain whether or not someone is biologically a male or female? What science is there? Because at the end of the day, men and women are, on average, made differently, which translates to different levels of strength, stamina, and other biologically driven factors. So I have conflicting opinions about this. I think I would have to see how this all turns out. I may have to eat my words, I may have to be grateful or I remain unconvinced.

Has your friend ever saved your life? My best friend, whose name I won’t disclose, once pulled me out of a blizzard. Not literally, of course, but the figurative equivalent. I was in a bad spot, spiralling downward, and he was the one who threw me a lifeline. He saw the storm brewing inside, the self-destructive tendencies taking hold. We’d known each other since we were kids, through thick and thin, the kind of friendship forged in shared experiences and youthful indiscretions. When I started going off the rails, he didn't judge, didn't preach. He simply acted, a quiet, unwavering presence. He didn't offer easy answers. Instead, he offered a different perspective, a challenge to my increasingly bleak worldview. He’d remind me of who I once was, the kid who used to dream big, the one who always saw the good in people. He’d gently nudge me back towards the path I was veering away from. Even if I resisted. Looking back, it's clear he saved me from myself. He showed me that even in the darkest storms, there’s always a glimmer of light. His actions spoke louder than words. He was the antithesis of the fair-weather friend. When everyone else disappeared, he stayed. He was a constant, a rock, someone I could lean on. It's a bond I cherish, a testament to the power of genuine friendship. He's a true mate, the type you'd follow to the ends of the earth.

Have you ever had a life-changing experience while working in fast food? I worked at McDonald's in high school. It was a grueling, soul-crushing job, not in a dramatic, romantic sense, but just in the relentless, repetitive nature of the work and the vapid, vacant expressions of my colleagues. I spent my days frying Filet-O-Fish, assembling Big Macs, and listening to the incessant beeping of the fryers. Honestly, I don’t believe it's possible for one to have any sort of life-changing experience in such an environment. I remember one shift when the deep fryer overflowed and nearly set the place ablaze. That was probably the most exciting event of my tenure. The customers, as you might expect, were a mixed bag. There were the perpetually grumpy, the overly demanding, and those who seemed genuinely afraid of the towering teenagers working behind the counter. I was a cashier, so I saw it all. From the endless stream of Happy Meals to the disgruntled patrons complaining about lukewarm fries, I had a front-row seat to the everyday theater of fast food. The shifts were long, the pay was lousy, and my uniform always seemed to be a magnet for ketchup stains. I’m pretty sure I could still tell you the complete list of ingredients in an Egg McMuffin if you woke me up at 3 in the morning. Despite the monotony, the experience wasn't entirely without merit. Namely that I learned the value of a hard-earned dollar, although it disappeared quickly into the abyss of gas money, movie tickets and fast food. I also learned a few basic life lessons such as never underestimate the power of a smile and always be polite, even when dealing with the most obnoxious customer. I'd say the job did not change my life, but gave me the necessary experience and a healthy dose of cynicism, something that has served me well in the years since.

What are some bad movies that could have worked by just having a better screenplay? One of the most glaring examples of this, in my opinion, is *The Adventures of Pluto Nash* (2002). The premise itself held promise. Who wouldn’t want to see Eddie Murphy as a moon-based nightclub owner in the year 2087, battling mobsters and robots? Sounds like a recipe for a fun, if not groundbreaking, sci-fi comedy, right? Wrong. The movie was a train wreck from start to finish. The special effects were atrocious even for the time, the direction was clunky, and the acting, while not the worst, was certainly not elevated by the material. But what really sunk the film was the atrocious screenplay. The jokes were stale, the plot was convoluted, and the characters were uninspired. It felt as if the writers just threw a bunch of ideas at the wall and hoped something would stick. What was supposed to be zany, quirky, and absurd came across as painfully unfunny and confusing. The film had a budget of $100 million and grossed a mere $7 million worldwide. It was a massive, embarrassing flop. I often wonder how different things might have been with a tighter, more comedic script. Even with its flaws, the basic concept of the film offered opportunities for greatness that were sadly squandered, never to be recovered. It could have been a cult classic, a guilty pleasure, but instead, it stands at the bottom of many movie lists, a testament to how a terrible script can ruin even the most promising of premises.

What's the biggest anticlimax in movie history? That’s a tricky one. Plenty of movies promise the earth and deliver a handful of pebbles. But for sheer, gut-wrenching letdown, I’d have to nominate the ending of *War of the Worlds* (2005). Sure, Spielberg’s take on the Martian invasion was visually spectacular, a masterclass in building tension and crafting genuinely terrifying scenes of global chaos. The destruction, the relentless pursuit, Dakota Fanning’s wide-eyed terror – all meticulously executed. But then, *poof*, everything is resolved by a conveniently acquired, and somewhat *deus ex machina*, virus. The relentless, overwhelming threat that had been so meticulously established evaporated in a matter of minutes. It's as if the writers panicked, realizing they'd painted themselves into a corner with no plausible escape route. You're left with a sense of profound dissatisfaction, a feeling that all the carefully constructed dread had been for naught. It's a textbook example of how a breathtaking build-up can be completely undermined by a rushed, uninspired resolution. And the thing is, in its inherent, frustrating simplicity, in its disappointing anti-climax, the ending perfectly mirrors the experience of watching countless other modern blockbusters. So, in a way, it became the ultimate commentary on the modern movie experience, a lesson in the frustrating allure of the cinematic tease. Perhaps the ending, in its sheer lack of imagination, captured a deeper truth, a truth about how so many movies dangle the promise of something grand only to give us the cinematic equivalent of a flat tire.

What’s your favorite movie based on true events? I'm a sucker for war movies, and there are few as harrowing and historically accurate as "Hacksaw Ridge" (2016). Its depiction of the Battle of Okinawa is unflinching, and Andrew Garfield's portrayal of Desmond Doss, the conscientious objector who saved countless lives without ever firing a shot, is nothing short of phenomenal. But there's a hidden gem of a true story that I love, "The Great Escape" (1963). Based on a real-life mass escape of Allied prisoners of war from a German POW camp during World War II, the film takes liberties with the facts, of course. However, it captures the daring spirit, ingenuity, and camaraderie of the men involved. Few people realize that the film, which made Steve McQueen a star, is only *loosely* based on the actual breach of the camp known as Stalag Luft III. The film's director, John Sturges, was an absolute genius: he masterfully crafted a suspenseful, thrilling, and emotionally resonant piece of cinema. While the film simplifies events, it doesn't sacrifice the essence of the story: a desperate attempt for freedom. All of this is in line with the spirit of the real-life events and the brave men who attempted to escape. And McQueen’s motorcycle jump? Pure Hollywood, but it *felt* real, and that’s what mattered. Did the Germans really chase McQueen on motorcycles? Of course not. Did the escapees really endure all the challenges displayed on screen? Of course not. And even though there’s a fair amount of embellishment, it still remains a powerful testament to the human spirit. The film's use of tension, humor, and, most importantly, the quiet dignity of the characters, elevates it beyond a simple action movie. It becomes a story about courage, resilience, and the unwavering belief in the possibility of freedom, even in the darkest of times. It's a movie you can watch again and again, picking up new details and appreciating the craft of filmmaking with each viewing. "The Great Escape" isn't just a war movie; it's a celebration of the human capacity for hope, even in the face of overwhelming odds.

As a teacher, have you ever been accused of something? Oh, lord, where to begin? Public school teaching is a minefield of potential accusations, simmering beneath the surface of every lesson plan and parent-teacher conference. It's a high-wire act, really, trying to balance the needs of thirty kids, the demands of the curriculum, and the expectations of a community often at odds with itself. You're constantly being scrutinized, your words and actions dissected for any hint of impropriety or bias. I’ve been teaching for over a decade, and I’ve seen it all. A parent once accused me of ‘indoctrinating’ her child with liberal propaganda, because I dared to suggest that the Earth was round and that slavery was bad. Another time, a student's mother claimed I was deliberately failing her son because I didn't give him an A despite his habitual tardiness and complete lack of effort. Of course, the most common accusation is some variation of ‘unfairness’. A student feels slighted by a grade, a comment, a seating arrangement, a perceived lack of attention. They go home, tell their parents, and suddenly you're facing a formal complaint, an investigation, or at the very least an awkward and uncomfortable meeting with the principal. It’s exhausting, to say the least. But you learn to develop a thick skin, to document everything meticulously, and to choose your battles wisely. You learn that not every accusation needs a response. Some you can shrug off, some you can try to reason with, and some you just have to accept as part of the job. The goal is not to be perfect, because that's impossible. The goal is to be fair, consistent, and to always act in the best interests of the students, even when those students and their parents are convinced you're out to get them.

Why do some people not like Coldplay? I've never had a problem with Coldplay. I’ve liked some of their music, not their entire discography but at least one or two songs in each of their albums. Their earlier stuff was better. I've always felt that Coldplay are a band that are unfairly maligned. It is not right to constantly use them as a punching bag for the music industry. I understand why people don't like them. Chris Martin's voice isn’t for everyone (I personally like it), their music can sound a bit similar, their lyrics can be vague, and their sound is considered ‘safe’. They’re not as edgy as Radiohead, as energetic as The Killers, as rebellious as Oasis, or as genre-bending as The Flaming Lips. They are a soft rock band who have made music which is usually pleasant enough to listen to on a road trip or while working in the office. The band’s success cannot be denied. They are the only band in recent times who, due to their popularity, can generate millions of dollars by performing at a concert anywhere on the planet. Whenever Coldplay releases a new album or is on global tour it is always headline news. The criticisms are always the same, almost boring. And there is always this sense of ‘hipster’ snobbery. In music and art there is always this desire to find the 'next' thing. The latest band that isn't trying too hard, that is too cool for school. Coldplay is not that. They are very much, mainstream. Some of them even go to the gym. Every time a band becomes popular everyone flocks to hate on them and everyone is doing it. And it is always a very tiresome thing to witness. There is a reason why Coldplay's fanbase is so massive all around the world. They make okay music and are not too difficult for almost anyone to listen to. I’m not a Coldplay fanatic, but I don’t get the constant vitriol. Music would be very boring indeed if every band sounded like Radiohead.

What show / movie had no right to be as good as it was? Let's go with *The Dark Knight*. I went in expecting a decent superhero movie, maybe a bit better than Batman Begins which I enjoyed. I was not expecting a cinematic masterpiece. From the opening bank heist to the final showdown in the hospital, every scene is meticulously crafted, brimming with tension and raw emotion. The casting is also perfect. Christian Bale brings a brooding intensity to Batman that's hard to match, Heath Ledger's performance as the Joker is simply iconic and the supporting roles from Michael Caine, Gary Oldman, and Aaron Eckhart are excellent. It’s a film that transcends the superhero genre, delving into themes of chaos, morality, and the corruption of power. The cinematography is superb, the score is haunting, and the direction by Christopher Nolan is flawless. I never thought a comic book adaptation could have such a profound impact on me. It's a movie I can watch over and over again, and each time I find something new to appreciate. It's a testament to what can be achieved when talent, vision, and a good budget align perfectly. There's no question it's a film for the ages. Batman should have stayed dead at the end.

Which actor played a villain role too well for comfort? Whenever I see Anthony Hopkins as Hannibal Lecter in The Silence of the Lambs, I cannot sleep properly for a good week. That’s not acting. That's sorcery. He didn’t play that role. He embodied it. In the movie, when Clarice Starling, played by Jodie Foster, first encounters him in the Baltimore Hospital for the Criminally Insane, he immediately makes his presence felt. Hopkins as Lecter looks straight at the camera with a predatory gaze that pierces the viewer's soul, a subtle smirk playing on his lips that makes you want to reach through the screen and slap it off his face. I've seen many movies where the antagonist is portrayed as a maniac, a raving lunatic with insane tics and all sorts of over-the-top idiosyncrasies. But Lecter is different. He's not maniacal. He is cunning, methodical and calculated in his cruelty. He possesses a charm that makes him all the more terrifying. He can be the life of the party, the one who always knows the right thing to say, and the one to get the room to burst with laughter, just like anyone else. But you know its all a facade, a calculated attempt to lure you to your doom. You know that the moment he gets the slightest whiff of a weakness in you, he will pounce on you ruthlessly. His polite, soft voice is a weapon more dangerous than any gun. He toys with Clarice, playing mind games with her, revealing just enough information to keep her hooked like a moth to a flame, all the while subtly probing her vulnerabilities. Even his body language is unsettling. The scene where he casually but precisely draws a sketch of the Florence cathedral while discussing murder is a masterclass in subtle menace. Every movement, every gesture is perfectly calibrated to create an atmosphere of dread. The way he licks his lips after saying "I ate his liver with some fava beans and a nice Chianti" is the stuff of nightmares. That performance has redefined the role of the villain in cinema forever.

What things do people say that make you roll your eyes? I am always taken aback by the self-professed "good guys" who flaunt acts of petty generosity. Do you hold a door open for someone? Expect a parade of gratitude? It's the bare minimum of human decency, not a display of sainthood. Likewise, the ceaseless virtue signaling that infests social media. An endless stream of "likes," comments, and shares designed to prove one’s moral superiority. It's exhausting.  Another eye-roller is the ubiquitous "bless your heart.” More often than not, it's a thinly veiled insult disguised as an expression of sympathy. It’s the linguistic equivalent of a gentle slap. And, of course, the unyielding positivity. The relentless insistence that everything is "amazing" or "the best day ever." It's a defense mechanism, a refusal to acknowledge the mundane or unpleasant realities of life. Life is not a constant highlight reel, and pretending it is makes me want to crawl back into my cave. Then there are those who begin most of their sentences with "Actually..." or "To be honest..." as if everything else they’ve ever uttered has been a work of fiction. Finally, the incessant comparisons to “back in my day." No one is interested in your tales of the good old days. Move on. The world keeps turning.

What's the most ridiculous thing a coworker told on you to your boss for? I’ve had a few jobs in my time but the most ridiculous thing a coworker ever attempted to do was a fabrication of events at a job I held where I delivered parcels and managed to somehow annoy one of my colleagues to a massive extent. I worked with a few people in that job, most of whom were fairly indifferent to my presence, but there was one guy who was something else. From day one he seemed to have my number. I’ve seen him have heated feuds previously with other members of staff. When I got the job I never knew why but I was apparently the recipient of his ire. One day I got called in by the boss to tell me that he had been informed that I was failing to wear gloves and was instead tossing parcels around like they were made of foam. This made me laugh. As much as being accused of ‘not wearing gloves’ is a minor offence it had the potential to be blown up and for the job to be done or I would have had to resign. The boss in question was an intelligent and level headed man, a good boss. He took the accusation with a grain of salt and asked me to explain my side of the story. I told the boss I was pretty certain this was a pack of lies. The boss said he would investigate before taking any action. I said my fellow workers were always complaining about the amount of work I did relative to what they did, which caused them some degree of jealousy which might have led to some malicious behavior. Sure enough the following day, the boss told me he had watched us doing our job and that this alleged complaint was absolute nonsense and in his words "complete and utter bullshit". He told me he had seen me wearing gloves, being careful with any parcels I came into contact with and being the hardest worker among everyone doing the delivery rounds. He told me he gave the colleague who reported me a stern talking to, which gave me an enormous amount of satisfaction. His name was called out and he would never be able to do in our presence that he was the one who caused my trouble. I wonder why I was the target of harassment from that guy. It could have arisen from a deep seeded self-hatred. It could have been the result of some form of competitive jealousy from him with me. It might have been that he was just a plain moron.

What red flag did you have right before a job offer that you wish you had heeded? I once interviewed for a position at a call center. During the interview the manager couldn't stop emphasizing how "family-oriented" the company was. Looking back, this should have been my first clue. The interviewer spent a disproportionate amount of time discussing company picnics, team-building exercises, and employee birthdays rather than the actual day-to-day responsibilities of the job. I've worked in many places, and there is a fine line between a healthy work environment and an unprofessional, cliquish one. My gut instinct told me that the latter was the case with this place. After I was offered the job, I was given a tour of the office and was surprised by the overall décor, it was like walking into a daycare center, complete with posters of smiling cartoon characters and inspirational quotes plastered everywhere. The workspaces were arranged in a way that facilitated constant interaction, which may be good for collaboration, but the lack of privacy would have driven an introvert such as myself to the brink of insanity. The second red flag came at the end of the tour. We walked past a small break room where a group of employees was huddled around a table, and the manager proudly announced, "We're all like one big family here!" They all turned and smiled at me, but there was an unsettling intensity in their collective gaze that made my skin crawl. I got the sense that this wasn't just a job; it was more like a cult. I should have listened to my instincts and run away. The third red flag came with the training. Days before the actual start date I was told to attend an all-day training session. The session started with a mandatory team bonding exercise, after which we took written tests on everything from customer service scripts to company policies. What surprised me was not the subject matter but the way in which the trainer berated the group on mistakes, using the same language a soccer coach used, who was berating his players. The whole environment felt suffocating, the pressure was on and there was little room for error. I did take the job but I left within a month. The experience left me with a profound sense of dread and the conviction that family-oriented companies are often just dysfunctional families in disguise.

What is an unpopular opinion you hold? In the digital age, I maintain that physical books are superior to e-readers. My aversion isn't rooted in some sentimental attachment to the musty scent of aged paper or the crinkle of turning a page. While I concede that the convenience of carrying an entire library in a sleek, backlit tablet is undeniable, the experience pales in comparison to the tactile joy of holding a bound volume in your hands. The weight, the texture of the cover, the way the spine molds to your grip – this is where the true immersion begins. It's not simply about reading; it's about the whole performance. The ritual. There's a certain focus that happens when you're not bombarded with notifications, social media updates, and the temptation to switch to a different app. A real book demands your undivided attention. You're less likely to skim, less likely to lose your place, less likely to develop those dreadful 'reading shortcuts' and more likely to truly digest the words on each page. The permanence of a physical copy also appeals to me. E-readers, by their fragile nature, by the constant pressure to upgrade, by the whims of corporate agendas, are inherently transient. A well-loved book, dog-eared and worn, is a testament to time spent, to ideas encountered, to a relationship formed. It is a companion. I understand the arguments for accessibility, for environmental concerns (though even the sustainability of e-readers has its critics) and for the sheer convenience of electronic devices, many times I succumb to its charm. However, let's not completely abandon the physical book, the analogue world.

What is that one picture that describes the lowest point in your life? I've never had a photograph taken of me, nor have I been one to take photographic records of my life. The closest I can get to answering this question would be to describe the images I could summon from my memory. The lowest point in my life would be the memory of spending the night, as a child, in a halfway house on my birthday. The memory is hazy and not as clear as I would like it to be. The place was cramped and run down. It wasn’t a place I would have ever volunteered to be in. It was a collection of rundown apartments, where the residents would change every few weeks. Some residents were alright, but the majority were dangerous or unpredictable. The living arrangements were a result of my parents’ divorce and my mother’s subsequent descent into depression and financial ruin. My birthday, like many days, was spent in the shadow of the fallout. I was a child and the memory is not as traumatic as my elder siblings. My birthday memory is more mundane. The low point about it was how unremarkable it truly was. I was told to stay put and behave. I was given a single slice of store bought birthday cake, a slice that was stale and did not taste good. The only present I received that day was a tattered, second-hand comic book that I read and re-read. It was not a happy birthday yet not an unpleasant one. The memory however is the photographic embodiment of a low point because it represents the mundane reality of the consequences I would experience. It represents a life uprooted, a life that didn’t work out the way it was supposed to. When looking at the memory I can recognize the circumstances and conditions I was in. I was neither abused nor neglected, but rather, I was just another kid in another forgotten place with little to no support, wondering how long before things got better.

Whom did you feel bad for in high school? I felt bad for the teachers. It's an understatement to say that high school was a formative period for me. Maybe it's because I am no longer in my teens and twenties but I look back with genuine fondness and happiness. My own memories are not always what they seem though. I don't remember working on my homework. I remember the parties, the girls, the music, the good times and the bad. I had my share of fights and I had my share of bullies. I had my share of academic disappointments and I had my share of successes. I was not one of the cooler kids. I was never going to be the Prom King. But I also wasn't a nerd or a geek. I was somewhere in the middle. The teachers were the ones who did the work. Dealing with the antics of teenagers is tough. I'm talking about the classroom, the hallways, the sports fields, the parking lot. I always felt bad when I was in trouble and the headmaster had to get involved. I always felt bad for the teachers who had to deal with me. They were always so nice to me. I was a good kid, mind you. I was never a troublemaker. I was not a delinquent. I was just a bit of a handful. I was restless and I was impatient. I got bored easily. I was always getting into mischief. Looking back it was an exhausting experience to teach us. They would be explaining the most basic of concepts to some of the students and it became obvious that some of us did not want to listen. They were doing overtime, working late into the night, grading papers, preparing lessons, dealing with parents, dealing with administrators, dealing with each other. A thankless job. They were always underpaid and underappreciated. It made some of the teachers bitter and angry. Some gave up. Some retired early.

Which supporting actress was much more memorable than the star of a movie? This is a tough one. In the movie *Thelma & Louise* (1991), Geena Davis was the lead and Susan Sarandon was the other lead, and both played the roles admirably. However, there's a small supporting role that overshadowed the two leads, and that was the role of Detective Hal Slocumb, played by Harvey Keitel. Not only was his performance brilliant, but he was also given the impossible task of trying to explain to the audience and the police force what was actually going on. He was tasked with making the audience feel empathy for two murderers, while not glorifying their crimes. With his understated manner, his calm presence, and just the sheer amount of screen time he had, he managed to do this. Sarandon and Davis were good, but Keitel was so much better. Another supporting actress who I thought outshone her lead was Jodie Foster in *Taxi Driver*(1976). Robert De Niro was, as usual, brilliant, but he played the main character, Travis Bickle, in a very restrained way, much to the movie’s brooding effect. Foster, on the other hand, played the child prostitute Iris with such precociousness and vulnerability that she stole every scene she was in. Granted, she was only 12 years old at the time. It was a brave decision by director Martin Scorsese to cast a child actor to play a challenging role, but it paid off handsomely. She was electrifying in her role. There are examples, however, where the lead actress is more memorable, such as Frances McDormand in *Fargo* (1996). William H. Macy was there, of course, and he was also brilliant as Jerry Lundegaard, but McDormand was the character that made the movie the classic that it is. Marge Gunderson will forever be remembered as one of the most iconic characters in cinema history.

What is the scariest moment you have had in your own home? I'm not much of a horror movie aficionado or a fan of the haunted house experience. I've always considered it to be a bit of a pantomime. A few years ago I was living in a small, rather dilapidated semi-detached house with a long, thin garden that backed onto a wooded area. The neighborhood was a quiet and friendly place, although a bit desolate, populated mostly by elderly people and young families. One night, I was home alone, working on my computer in the living room. The only sounds were the gentle hum of the computer fan and the distant, muted noises from the television in the background. I usually kept the windows closed, but this evening it had been a warm day, so I’d opened one slightly in order to get some air circulation in the room. I heard a faint scratching sound coming from the hallway. At first, I dismissed it as the house settling or some sort of plumbing issue. It wasn't all that unusual. But the scratching continued, more insistent this time, and it was steadily getting closer. My heart started to pound against my ribcage, and I felt a cold shiver run down my spine. I sat perfectly still, listening intently. The scratching was now right outside the door. The door was an old, wooden affair with a glass panel at the top, and my imagination ran wild, picturing a clawed hand scraping against the glass, a distorted silhouette looming there. I froze, unable to move, my mind conjuring up images of a shadowy figure just waiting on the other side to burst in. I took a deep breath and, slowly, I decided to get up and investigate. I inched toward the door, my hand outstretched, ready to grab the handle if I needed to make a quick getaway. I stood there for what seemed like an eternity, paralyzed by fear. With my hand resting on the lock, I slowly turned the handle and opened the door. There, in the dim light of the hallway, was a small, stray kitten, pawing gently against the door. The scratching was its little claws seeking a way in. I was so relieved I actually laughed out loud, a sound that broke through the tension. The kitten looked up at me, blinked its big, innocent eyes, and then, as if nothing had happened, padded into the living room and began to explore its new surroundings. I fed it some milk and, eventually, it curled up on the sofa and fell asleep. My scariest home moment, and it was delivered by a tiny, furry marauder. I still have the cat.

Can you provide some examples of average actors delivering great performances due to well-written characters? Absolutely. There are countless instances of performers transcending their usual limitations when gifted with a character rich in nuance and depth. Take, for instance, the role of Lester Burnham in *American Beauty*. Kevin Spacey, though his performance was universally lauded and deservedly won him an Oscar, wasn’t necessarily known for his emotionally raw portrayals prior to this film. The intricate layers of self-loathing, repressed desire, and ultimately, liberation, allowed him to deliver a performance that is both deeply unsettling and strangely sympathetic. The writing, that of Alan Ball, provided a blueprint for a character that could plumb the depths of mid-life crisis with an unflinching gaze. Similarly, consider the trajectory of Robert De Niro in *Taxi Driver*. While De Niro is undeniably a powerhouse, his transformation into Travis Bickle, a disturbed Vietnam veteran driving a cab through the nocturnal underbelly of New York City, is nothing short of remarkable. The script, penned by Paul Schrader, gave De Niro the fodder to explore alienation, loneliness, and the descent into violent psychosis. It's a testament to the symbiotic relationship between a compelling character and an actor who can bring it to life. Another excellent example is Heath Ledger as the Joker in *The Dark Knight*. Although Ledger was already achieving prominence, the complexity of the Joker, as envisioned by Christopher Nolan and fleshed out by the late actor in his performance, allowed him to embody pure chaos. It was a character simultaneously hilarious, terrifying, and utterly unpredictable, allowing him to showcase a range previously unseen in the actor. The screenplay’s mastery was crucial in crafting a villain whose motivations remained shrouded in mystery. It's also important to note how a well-written character can elevate the performance of an actor who might be considered a niche character actor or even a character actor on the periphery. Take, for example, Christoph Waltz's portrayal of Colonel Hans Landa in *Inglourious Basterds*. Though already a seasoned performer in various European productions, Landa marked his breakthrough role on American audiences. Without the character's razor-sharp wit, linguistic prowess, and chilling cunning, Waltz’s inherent talent wouldn’t have had the same opportunity to shine.

Have you ever had a co-worker who you worked closely with get fired for something truly shocking that you never saw coming? Absolutely. I once worked with a guy named Barry at a local bookstore, a real bookworm if there ever was one. Barry and I were practically joined at the hip, shelving books, assisting customers, and commiserating over the eccentricities of our boss, a woman who seemed to have stepped straight out of a Dickens novel. One day, as we were stocking the new releases, Barry received a phone call. He turned ashen, his hand trembling so violently that he nearly dropped a signed copy of a Salman Rushdie. After a brief, strained conversation, he slammed down the phone, mumbled something about needing a break, and disappeared. Hours later, our manager informed me that Barry had been terminated, effective immediately. The reason? Embezzlement. Embezzlement! Can you believe it? Barry, a man who seemed more likely to donate his paycheck to a library than steal a dime, was accused of siphoning funds from the store. I could hardly process it. The police were involved, investigations, the whole shebang. Barry, the gentle giant of literature, busted for a crime that felt utterly alien to his character. It turns out, he had a gambling problem, a secret life of high-stakes poker games and mounting debts. The money he stole from the store – a pittance, really, when you consider the scale of his habit – was meant to cover his losses. It was a classic case of addiction spiraling out of control, a fall from grace that shook everyone who knew him. To see a person you thought you knew crumble so completely, so swiftly, was a truly disorienting experience. It was an example of how little we really know about each other. We never saw it coming, not in a million years.

If all animals were horse-sized, which would be the most majestic to ride into battle? The elephant, undoubtedly. Not the elephant of some antiquated, dusty history book, but a modern, combat-ready behemoth. Picture it: a magnificent, grey-skinned giant, its massive frame clad in gleaming, reinforced steel plating, a war-saddle of braided leather and titanium alloys firmly affixed to its back. The air crackles with the hum of advanced weaponry integrated into its frame – perhaps strategically placed laser cannons or even a shoulder-mounted railgun for dealing with particularly pesky adversaries. The mahout, a seasoned warrior clad in futuristic armor, is one with the beast, directing it through the chaos, and navigating the battlefield with a commanding presence. This isn't a mere steed; it's a mobile fortress, a symbol of unwavering power and undeniable intimidation. A creature that crushes the skull of its foes with its forelegs and then unleashes a storm of fire upon them. The ground trembles as this equine titan thunders towards the enemy lines, a walking embodiment of force, leaving a trail of destruction and awe in its wake. Think of the sheer psychological impact: the demoralizing terror that would grip your opponents as they witness this juggernaut bearing down upon them. Imagine the stories that would be told, the legends that would be forged, around this magnificent, terrifying spectacle: a war elephant, re-imagined for a future of conflict. The ultimate war machine.

What is the most obnoxious thing you have seen someone do at the grocery store? I witnessed a woman, let's just say she was of a certain age, deliberately cough all over the open produce bin, and when I say cough, I mean she was engaged in a full-bodied, convulsive, phlegm-laden hacking session. This occurred with theatrical flourish. She then proceeded to inspect the affected fruits and vegetables with laser-like precision. This prompted a store employee, a young lad with the unfortunate luck of working on a slow Tuesday afternoon, to approach and inquire if everything was all right. This woman responded with a glare that could curdle milk, informing the employee in a voice that could shatter glass that she was "merely selecting the freshest specimens." The employee, a picture of suppressed outrage, attempted to clear the area, informing nearby customers of the situation. The woman, however, took this, not as a defeat, but as a challenge. She continued about her business, deliberately handling and even squeezing items. Her demeanor suggested that she took great pleasure in the ensuing panic. The young fellow, visibly mortified, seemed to have just accepted his fate. I’m still appalled at the sheer audacity of that woman. What I find most egregious wasn’t necessarily the health risk she was creating, but the fact she appeared to revel in causing discomfort and inconvenience to everyone around her. Some people are just like that I guess: pure, unadulterated jerks.

What is the lamest “benefit” you’ve been offered by an employer? I worked as an usher in a major multiplex cinema. The kind of role where I was paid minimum wage and was expected to do the work of four people. They had a ‘benefit’ program to reward us for our hard work, one that was presented as ‘special’ when in reality it was a sick joke. We were rewarded with… wait for it… a free small popcorn and a small soda *once* a week! Which, if you knew the price of those items, one could hardly call a benefit. It would cost the cinema very little, yet they acted like they were bestowing upon us the riches of Croesus himself. I, along with other fellow employees, would get laughed at for even bringing it up as a topic of conversation. It’s not that we didn’t appreciate it. Not in the slightest. It was just insulting. We, of course, could watch a movie as a benefit, but that was it. Nothing else to bring in the money. Considering how ridiculously cheap it was to run the cinema, offering us the occasional free popcorn and soda was considered by management to be a great gesture of appreciation. But it wasn’t. It was a slap in the face. It was like they were saying, ‘You’re not worth anything more than this. Now get back to cleaning up those mountains of trash!’ It left a sour taste in my mouth, and I always felt undervalued afterward. It was a masterclass in how to demoralize employees.

What is your 10-year gap photo? I’m not a big one for taking a photo every year. I have a terrible memory. Also, I don't think it's particularly useful. Not in the long-term. I've only done it once. Back in 2013 a friend of mine, an absolute film buff, persuaded me to watch Before Sunrise (1995), along with its two sequels, Before Sunset (2004) and Before Midnight (2013). The second movie occurs nine years after the first and the third one, a further nine years after that, hence the 10-year gap photos the actors chose to do. I loved the films. As a film trilogy, it’s probably the most realistic portrayal of aging in love with a partner. I have a couple of photos from the past that I treasure. One from 1994. Back when I first met my wife. She looks so incredibly youthful. And the other one, back from 2013. My wife and I were in one of our more happier moments. I always make sure that the photographs will show me in a positive light. What’s the point of taking a photo, as a memento, if you are going to remember that you looked bloated, unhappy and dishevelled? But apart from this, I don't have any recent photos. I’m more likely to be on the phone or the computer, wasting time on the internet, than standing in front of a camera. I do have a profile photo on my various computer, but they’re usually old. The same goes for my phone. I’m more likely to have a photo on my phone of my dog. I have a photo of the dog taken at the vets back in 2018. He looked such an utter disgrace. This photo has become something of an inner-joke between my wife and I, that we tend to laugh about every now and again. So I don't really have a ‘ten year gap’ photo but the one photo that stands out in my memory is, as I’ve said, is from that dog photo at the vets. He looked that bad.

At what age did you stop enjoying YA fiction? I never really got into YA fiction. I was a child when YA fiction was coming into its own. I was reading The Lord of the Rings and John Grisham before I even started middle school. I vaguely recall a few books from the Goosebumps franchise (I remember being particularly scared of *Say Cheese and Die!*). I did enjoy a few books from the Choose Your Own Adventure series but I didn't consider it to be 'literature'. In my teens I was firmly into ‘cool’ books or what I perceived to be cool books: novels of the Modernists, Beatniks, Existentialists and the so called ‘literary’ authors. I'd browse and read whatever I could get on free library. I was too proud to let my friends know what books I was reading, but also too socially awkward to discuss books with my friends. When I was younger I would sit in the library and pore over books. I would lose track of time and space, reading for several hours. I did the same thing later on at university/college. I'd hole up and read for hours. The biggest difference was that when I was kid, I was searching for books. At university/college I was searching for thoughts and concepts that helped me understand life, myself and the world. I have always been into reading and research, so maybe that is why I never really got into reading YA fiction. There was very little overlap of subject matter and interests between myself and the YA audience. I was also way too impatient for the plot to pick up. Most YA fiction books I skimmed through took way too long to arrive at any interesting point. I will read YA fiction if it is on a list given by a high school teacher if I truly respect the teacher. But I will also most of the time take my assigned kid to the latest Marvel Superhero movie. Even Spider-Man: Into the Spider-Verse beats most of Hollywood movies.

Who is the best classic rock drummer? It’s easy to say John Bonham, Neil Peart, or Keith Moon. And while they're all worthy of the title, it feels a bit like a cheat to instantly name the most obvious contenders. I’d have to say Levon Helm. Why? Well, first of all, he was a great singer. He provided some real grit to The Band's sound. That would be the first attribute. Second of all is that he had that indefinable quality of 'swing'. No matter how complex his playing was, it always had a natural, almost effortless feel. Listening to him you could hear the blues and the gospel and the country influences, which is to say that he was a drummer who had absorbed American roots music. His playing was never about flashy solos or technical pyrotechnics, but it was always imaginative, musical, and perfectly suited to the song. His drumming was very much about the song, and he was utterly selfless in his approach. No one played for themselves. This is in evidence in the way The Band would cover any genre of music with absolute ease. In the process they would still keep their sound. They were a unique and cohesive unit. Each member was essential. They were more than the sum of their parts. Each member could have been a star on their own but here they were supporting each other. His work with The Band, whether it was the raucous energy of "The Weight," the simple drive of "Up on Cripple Creek," or the complex arrangements of "The Night They Drove Old Dixie Down," stands as some of the most influential drumming in the history of rock. If you're looking for proof, listen to any of their albums, and listen closely to what Levon is doing back there. He’s the glue that holds the songs together. In the best possible way, his drumming wasn't just about the beat or the rhythm; it was about the feel. He was a master of groove, a musician with absolute integrity, and a cornerstone of one of the most important bands in rock and roll history.

Why are so many men scared to date single mothers? I've always found the question a little perplexing, truth be told. I am, after all, a man, but I've never harbored any particular aversion to the prospect. One might, perhaps, venture a guess that it stems from the perceived 'baggage' – the ex-partner, the financial responsibilities, and the overall emotional complexities that often accompany raising a child solo. It's easy to imagine a scenario where a potential suitor might hesitate, envisioning a life of constant obligations and potential drama.  However, I'm inclined to believe the root goes deeper than that. I suspect some men might be intimidated by the perceived strength and resolve of a single mother. Let's face it; raising a child, especially without a partner, is an incredibly challenging undertaking. It requires resilience, resourcefulness, and an unwavering commitment to the child's well-being. A man might question his ability to 'measure up' to such standards, fearing that he wouldn't be able to provide the kind of stability and support the situation demanded. Still other men may have issues with the child not being "theirs," but a product of a previous relationship, not their own 'flesh and blood' as it were. Then there is the whole issue of a man's machismo. Some men may consider it "a blow" to their ego that they couldn't 'win' a woman over before she already had children. And of course in a society where the traditional roles of men and woman are still defined by a patriarchal lens, there's the implicit assumption that relationships follow an archetypal script. The single mother diverges from the traditional structure - the narrative of finding love between two people and then finding ways to raise children. It requires you, as the new partner, to occupy a place in an established family unit--a unit built around the other man, the child's father. A man may subconsciously resent not being the 'first.' He might not feel like the 'real man,' but merely a support figure. Many men, it would seem, are more prone to self-doubt rather than being the rock that such women so desperately need.

What is the biggest lie society has taught you to believe? That the truth is always good. I'm a bit cynical, I know, but hear me out. Growing up, we're bombarded with platitudes about honesty being the best policy, that white lies are somehow worse than cold, hard truths, and that the world bends over backwards for those who "tell it like it is." Bullshit. Utter, unadulterated bullshit. Sometimes, the truth is a wrecking ball, a screaming siren that shatters everything around it. Sometimes, the truth is a scalpel wielded by someone with ulterior motives, carving away at the delicate tissue of relationships or societal structures. And sometimes, tragically, the truth is just plain boring. So, we pretend. We embellish. We build narratives that soothe the savage beast of reality. We are all, to some degree, liars. Not malicious deceivers, mind you, but architects of personal mythology. Without the capacity to bend the truth, to reframe the narrative, to tell ourselves—and others—what we need to hear, we'd all be living in a state of perpetual psychic wreckage. Think about it: the well-meaning friend who assures you your new haircut looks "great," even though you look like a startled poodle; the loved one who glosses over a painful memory to spare your feelings; the politician who promises prosperity while secretly shuffling money into their own offshore accounts. Those are a different breed of lie, perhaps, but they exist because the unfettered truth can be a destructive force. The biggest lie society has taught me? That honesty alone will set you free. It won't. It will most likely get you exiled. So, I'll keep telling my own truths. After all, as the saying goes, a little bit of falsehood goes a long way.

Were you popular in high school? I was not. I'm not even what you would call ‘unpopular.’ I was just there. Inconspicuous. The sort of person you’d walk right past in the hallway without a second glance to the point of being invisible. I was the kind of kid who was always happy to sit at the back of the classroom and shut up and keep to myself. The only reason I knew my classmates was because they were forced to be in class with me and not because I had any friends. I was fine with this. I didn't feel any sense of loneliness or alienation. I came from a working-class family and there were certain practical responsibilities that came with that. I needed to study, pass my exams, get a good job and look after my family. The pressures of social standing and peer acceptance frankly seemed like a waste of time. I suppose there were occasions where I noticed the popular kids mocking or bullying others but to be honest I was too focused on my own work to pay attention to them. The most memorable time I’ve ever interacted with the popular kids in school was when I was forced to be in a group project with them in History class. I remember we were tasked with writing a group essay on Napoleon. Everyone in the group knew that I knew far more about Napoleon than they did which came as no surprise as I used to read about him constantly. It was either Napoleon or World War 2, those were the only things that interested me. I remember trying to contribute my ideas to the project. I provided arguments about Napoleon's military tactics, statecraft etc but every time I spoke I was mocked and ridiculed. They insisted on using a totally different approach. After a few minutes I decided that I was not going to waste my time explaining ideas to people who didn't want to listen. In the end I wrote the entire essay myself and they received a free ride. My work was praised by the teacher. Their contribution was zero. Edit: Sorry for the lengthy answer. Just trying give a good answer for the questions that have been posed.

What are some inaccuracies or criticisms of JD Vance's book "Hillbilly Elegy"? Though I am not a fan of "Hillbilly Elegy", to say that it's wildly inaccurate is also an overstatement. It's more correct to say that the book lacks a certain degree of nuance, and is far too broad and sweeping in its generalisations. Vance's main claim is that the white working class has become culturally and economically stagnant due to a lack of ambition and inherent familial dysfunction. However, he never fully acknowledges how poverty stricken communities in Appalachia have undergone sustained economic and social decline due to corporate malfeasance and the disastrous effects of the opioid epidemic. Vance's own family were by no means saints (the author himself admits to the dysfunctional nature of his bloodline) but he doesn’t highlight or give any serious weight to the external pressures that impacted their lives. Another criticism leveled by the book is that he spends too little time looking into the economic drivers of the region's decline. The decline of job opportunities after the collapse of the coal industry is not given the attention it deserves. Many point out that that the book reads as a one-sided argument with the author himself being the protagonist and all the other characters being peripheral caricatures. Vance positions himself as a hero, a person who extracted himself from a life of poverty, drug use and lack of opportunity. His critics point out that this narrative is a rather self-serving one. There's a lot more to say.

What's the most obnoxious instance of America-centric behavior you've ever witnessed? I once had the displeasure of sharing a hotel elevator with a group of Americans. I'm not one for making generalisations, but these specimens were the epitome of the Ugly

What are some of the biggest casting blunders in Hollywood movies? There are so many to choose from. The biggest casting blunder doesn't necessarily mean the performance was bad. It's when the actor or actress cast is so wrong for the part that it totally jars the audience and takes them out of the movie. For example, the casting of Mickey Rooney as Mr. Yunioshi in Breakfast at Tiffany's. Not only was the performance racially insensitive, but the very idea of a Caucasian actor, even a diminutive one like Rooney, playing a Japanese character in a movie released in 1961 is simply mind-boggling. It’s a relic of a bygone era when Hollywood didn't care about representation and diversity. Another example would be casting Emma Stone as a part-Asian character in Aloha. It's an issue that continues to plague Hollywood, where skin color, facial features, and ethnic background are considered secondary to box office appeal. However, for sheer wrongness, I'd have to nominate the casting of John Wayne as Genghis Khan in The Conqueror (1956). The film was already historically inaccurate and culturally insensitive, but the choice of John Wayne, a quintessential American cowboy, to play a Mongolian warlord was the coup de grâce. It’s so bad that it's almost good. I can't help but laugh whenever I see it. It's a perfect example of Hollywood's cluelessness and disregard for cultural sensitivity. The movie was a box office bomb, and it also gained notoriety for its production history, which unfortunately, was related to the surrounding nuclear testing done nearby. Some of the cast and crew later contracted cancer, with Wayne himself succumbing to it. All of this could have been avoided if he'd never taken the role, but I digress. Casting blunders are a fascinating indicator of Hollywood's evolution, its failures, and, sometimes, its surprising successes.

What's the dumbest thing you've gotten in trouble for at school? In elementary school, I got into a spot of bother for attempting to trade a classmate a plastic army man for her orange. The teacher, Miss Crabtree (not her real name...I think), was a stickler, the sort who would gleefully confiscate your favourite Pokemon card for the heinous crime of letting it slightly peek out of your binder. She saw the whole exchange, of course, from the vantage point only she could see: the front of the classroom where she lorded over us all. I was a scrawny kid, maybe seven or eight, with a penchant for the ludicrous and an unshakeable belief that everything was negotiable. I'm not entirely certain what drove me to pursue this particular transaction. Maybe it was the allure of the forbidden – fruit was only permitted during lunchtime, so a midday orange held a certain mystique. Or perhaps it was the sheer audacity of the exchange itself, the thrill of attempting to subvert the rigid rules of the classroom. Whatever the reason, I approached the girl with all the cunning a seven-year-old could muster. I offered the army man, a green, plastic soldier frozen mid-stride, rifle at the ready. The girl, a sweet-faced child with pigtails, seemed to consider it. I could see the wheels turning in her young mind. But then Miss Crabtree pounced, and the deal was off.

Who won the first 2024 debate between Trump and Biden? My gut tells me that nobody won. Just a hunch though. I did not watch the debate. It’s like the NFL Super Bowl. At the end of the day there’s only one winner which is not related to what happened on the field: The broadcast companies. They make money regardless of whether the game is riveting or a bore. Same with the debates. The viewership numbers matter most. Trump and Biden are simply the actors in the drama. I presume the debate commission, the moderators, the news analysts, the political pundits and their sponsors all did not lose. They have all won, no matter how the debate unfolded. Even the audience who got to witness the events did not lose. They get to sit back, relax, watch two old men go back and forth, and then smugly go about their days talking about how they would have done better while being blissfully unaware that if they were in the same position they would be in a worse situation. In some ways, after the Trump-Biden faceoff, we can't blame them. The ones who lose will be the ones who genuinely cared but were already conflicted by the current state of things. The ones who invested their emotional well-being and now feel even more lost and disenfranchised. The ones who looked upon the country and only saw decay and decline. The ones who looked forward to the future and saw nothing. I don’t have to watch the debate to be aware of such.

What is the common parenting mistake and how can they rectify that? Every parent, at some point, stumbles and commits what, in hindsight, they recognize as a blunder. One of the most common mistakes is the failure to remain consistent with boundaries. Kids are remarkably adept at pushing limits and exploiting any perceived inconsistency in parental expectations. A parent might decree no video games during the week, then, after a particularly trying day, cave and allow an hour, creating a confusing message. Children thrive on predictability; they need to know where the lines are drawn. When those lines shift, it causes insecurity and confusion. Parents must establish clear, unwavering rules and enforce them consistently, lest they undermine their authority and leave the kids feeling they are in charge. Another widespread misstep is the tendency to over-schedule children. In an effort to provide their offspring with every advantage, parents often sign them up for a laundry list of activities: sports, music lessons, tutoring, et cetera. This leaves little room for unstructured play and downtime, which are vital for creativity, social development, and the simple joy of being a kid. The rectification lies in scaling back. Prioritizing a few core activities and leaving plenty of space for free time allows children to pursue their own interests, develop self-reliance, and simply breathe. Finally, many parents fall into the trap of focusing exclusively on external accomplishments: grades, awards, athletic prowess. They equate these measures of success with their child’s worth. It fosters a sense of conditional love, where the child feels they must constantly perform to earn their parent’s approval. The solution is to emphasize effort, character, and kindness over achievement. Praise the child's resilience when they fail, their compassion for others, and their willingness to try, irrespective of results. This shift in focus fosters self-esteem, resilience, and the understanding that their value resides not in what they do, but in who they are. These aren't the only common mistakes, nor are they easy fixes. But by recognizing these pitfalls and striving for more consistent boundaries, balanced schedules, and a focus on intrinsic worth, parents can create a more supportive and nurturing environment for their children.

Do you think Europe is more racist than the USA? That's a loaded question, isn't it? It's like asking whether a viper is more venomous than a cobra—both will mess you up, just in different ways. Europe and the USA have fundamentally different histories, and that shapes their relationships with race in ways that are nearly impossible to directly compare. The US, forged in the crucible of slavery and segregation, carries the scars of its original sin on its sleeve. Systemic racism is embedded in the very fabric of its institutions and culture, a constant reminder of a past that refuses to stay buried. Europe, on the other hand, grapples with its colonial past, a legacy of exploitation and dominance that created a "them" versus "us" dynamic with people from all over the world on all of its continents. This has mutated into a form of racism not necessarily aimed at a given race, but a form of nationalism that has existed since the formation of the nation state and the rise of empires. This is more subtle, a slow burn of prejudice that is also constantly being exacerbated by its own problems. The US has the advantage of being a constant melting pot of cultures where immigration is part of its ethos. Europe has to deal with the problem of integrating people of cultures and creeds that it has never had to do before. With all that said, both territories have plenty of skeletons in the closet and a long way to go when it comes to genuine racial equality. Both are hotbeds of hypocrisy depending on which way the prevailing winds blow. To put it another way, comparing the two is like playing a game of "who's got it worse?" While a useful exercise to an extent, it is one that completely misses the bigger picture. Neither side is exempt from the responsibility of confronting their own demons, but they can’t do it by pointing fingers and downplaying their problems.

Who is the most underestimated horror movie villain? I'd have to give that dubious honor to the creature from *It Follows*. Not the clown from *It*, not Freddy Krueger from *Nightmare on Elm Street*, not even the creepy little girl from *The Ring*. Those are all formidable and chilling villains, to be sure, but they often rely on jump scares or a specific, established mythology to frighten the audience. The monster from *It Follows* is unique in its simplicity and its relentlessly slow, methodical pursuit. It doesn't jump out at you, it doesn't have any discernible supernatural powers beyond its ability to shape-shift, nor does it require any specific ritual or location to inflict its terror. It's a monster that’s always there, sometimes recognizable, sometimes not, always a harbinger of certain doom, moving slowly but inexorably closer and the more frightening when you take into consideration its utter lack of motivation or malice. It simply *follows*. The fear it instills is not based on gore or shock value, but on a primal sense of dread and the helplessness that comes with knowing you are being stalked by something you cannot outrun, fight, or even fully understand. It is an invisible killer that is always on the verge of revealing itself. What amplifies the psychological dread it exerts is that the protagonist's safety depends on the actions of others. When the protagonist gets infected, the threat becomes the people that she loves; friends, family, the people who give her protection. The longer she lives the more the risk that her friends and family will be infected or killed. It is a masterclass in slow-burn horror, using the power of suggestion and impending dread to create a truly unsettling and unforgettable cinematic experience. It’s a monster you can't hide from, can't reason with and can't escape.

What was the kindest thing someone did for you when you were young? My grandparents, originally from a small village in rural Trinidad, had a penchant for sending us care packages from home, filled with goodies we could never find in the supermarkets of London. These weren't just any old treats. We're talking about the good stuff: freshly roasted coffee, still warm from the roasting, fragrant mangoes when they were in season, and home-baked doubles, lovingly spiced with a secret blend of herbs and spices. These packages, arriving at our doorstep, became more than just deliveries; they were a lifeline, a tangible connection to a world of vibrant colours, potent smells and unique flavors that we rarely experienced in our grey existence. It was a burst of warmth in stark contrast to the cold, rainy English weather. Aside from the edible delights there was a whole kaleidoscope of family news, gossip and village happenings. It helped us. Made us feel less alone. And the real joy of the care packages were not the treats themselves, but the fact that my grandparents made an effort to source the best and send them. We were in their thoughts and they wanted us to feel loved and cared for. They would go to tremendous lengths to secure them for us. They had a small, basic bungalow home and the journey to procure these items would take a full day. We were raised in a modest home with a single income and would have struggled to survive. So in a very roundabout way we had very little. Our parents did the best that they could with their financial burdens. But through the simple act of sending care packages, my grandparents somehow managed to provide those small joys, which ultimately spoke volumes. These packages served as a constant reminder of home and family. I look back at the moment when I saw the contents of the package. That gesture of generosity, that simple act of love, is a memory I'll always cherish. It was a constant reminder of how much our grandparents loved us from a far away place.

I'm a school custodian and when people ask me what's my job I'm ashamed to tell them. What's the best way I could say what I do without saying I'm a custodian? The problem isn’t the job itself. It’s the association, the implication that comes along with it. When people hear "custodian," they immediately picture the guy with the mop and bucket, the one who cleans up after everyone else. You know, the unsung hero who's scraping gum off desks and scrubbing toilets. The thing is, there's far more to it than that. I’m not saying that being a custodian is a bad thing, but the way some people look at you, there's a subtle condescension. You’re the janitor, the cleaner, the guy who gets paid to take care of the mess other people make. And usually, that’s exactly the job. So, what's the best way to describe my profession to avoid the usual baggage that accompanies the word "custodian"? Well, I could opt for the obvious. "I'm in facilities management," or "I'm a building maintenance worker." Those sound a bit more formal, a bit more respectable. But they also feel a little… bland, devoid of character. It’s like trying to impress someone by saying you're an “aviation specialist” instead of a pilot. I could also use a bit of humor. “I’m the guy who's always cleaning up after the party." Or,  "I'm a professional mess-remover". Something that acknowledges the reality of the job while still making light of it. Still, it's always in the back of your mind: what will they think? What are they really thinking? If they knew the truth of what you did every day - the real dirt, literally and figuratively – would they offer such a casual dismissal of your work? Maybe an embellishment is in order: "I ensure the school is a clean and safe environment." Or a more accurate – though wordy - description: "I provide the upkeep and maintenance of the school's physical structures." But really, it’s not about the words; it’s about confidence. It’s about how you present yourself. After a while I learned to say, "I'm a custodian in a school," and wear it as a badge of honor, a reminder that I'm responsible for the neat, clean, well-organized experience of the people who come through those doors. Still, the initial question is a good one. How to impress when you are working a thankless job?

Why is a bronze medal winner happier than a silver medal winner? What is counterfactual thinking? The effect is quite dramatic. The bronze medal winner is happier because they are comparing themselves to somebody who didn't win a medal at all, therefore they are happier to have got something rather than nothing. Meanwhile, the silver medal winner is comparing themselves to the gold medal winner: They were so close. They were first. They could have had it all. This is known as counterfactual thinking. This is the act of mentally undoing something that happened in the past. When a situation does not go the way we expect, that negative outcome produces a state of cognitive dissonance. We mentally rehash the situation, asking "what if?" What if I did this instead of that? What if I said this to them? What if I had only trained harder? This often leads to regret, frustration, and other negative emotions. This is why a silver medal winner can look so disappointed. They would be going over the race in their head, thinking how they could have won the gold, and this would likely lead to them being less happy than the bronze medal winner. Counterfactual thinking can be both beneficial and destructive. It can be beneficial because it highlights how we can learn from our mistakes and avoid making those same mistakes again in the future. However, it can also cause significant psychological distress. When we obsess over our mistakes, it can negatively impact our mental health, leading to increased feelings of sadness, anxiety, and depression. Also as a Conservative who’s also a devotee of the ‘self help’ philosophy, the act of counterfactual thinking can stop all of this in its tracks. It is a waste of time. There's no point in thinking what might have been or should have been. It is what it is. Deal with it and move on. No matter how devastating it may be there is still some tiny measure of peace to be had in this world.
