What is the smallest scam you have ever seen? I wouldn't call it a "scam" per se, but I did see something rather audacious happen at a local bowling alley when I was a teenager. This particular establishment had a rather dilapidated arcade area. You know the kind - the same ancient Pac-Man and Galaga machines that have been making the rounds since the early 80s, coupled with a few newer, flashier games that were invariably out of order. There was this one game, a racing game, that was perpetually broken. The steering wheel was either completely unresponsive or it would spin uncontrollably, sending your car careening off the track faster than you could blink. One day, I witnessed a couple of older kids, maybe 16 or 17, expertly working the game – or at least, pretending to. One would distract the teenage attendant, pointing at a non-functioning pinball machine and feigning interest. The other would stand at the racing game, furiously manipulating the broken steering wheel in a manic fashion, as if he were actually controlling the car. He would shout, making engine noises and simulating near misses, and all the while, the game’s internal clock continued to tick, charging the pair for time spent. They played this game for all of 15 minutes, or so it seemed, before casually walking off; neither had put a single coin into the machine. The attendant never caught a glimpse of the trickery since he was occupied. I'm betting that there were a few bucks worth of credits rung up, credits they never paid for. What was probably a couple dollars scam, maximum. I remember thinking at the time, “How utterly, spectacularly pointless.” They probably could’ve earned the same amount of money collecting cans from the bowling alley trash bin. It was just a small act of petty larceny, born, I suspect, of boredom and a desire to see if they could get away with it. They did, of course. I still remember the look on their faces as they sauntered away, a mixture of brazen amusement. It was the kind of small-scale chicanery that makes you shake your head and sigh, not because you're shocked by the audacity of it all, but because you're perplexed by the sheer insignificance of the endeavor. A truly pathetic display.

What are the wrong depictions of the US in Hollywood movies? I've always found a peculiar contradiction when it comes to Hollywood's portrayal of the US, specifically the concept of the 'American Dream.' On the one hand, you have movies that depict the US as this land of boundless opportunity, where anyone can rise from rags to riches with enough grit and gumption. These films often showcase the glitz and glamour, the sprawling mansions, and the fast cars, creating this almost mythical image of success that's available to all. You see it in countless rags-to-riches stories, feel-good dramas, or even comedies where an underdog unexpectedly triumphs against all odds. The inherent message is optimistic, fueling the idea that America is the ultimate meritocracy, where hard work and determination are all you need to achieve your loftiest goals. However, a stark contrast emerges when you delve into the darker, more critical films. These movies offer a more cynical view exposing the underbelly of American society. They highlight the corruption, the vast economic disparities, and the systemic barriers that make the American Dream unattainable for many. You see it in gritty crime dramas, social commentaries, and independent films focusing on the lives of the marginalized. In these narratives, the American Dream often feels like a cruel delusion, a carrot dangled in front of the working class they can never reach. There's this constant clash between the idealistic image and the harsh reality, which is compounded by the constant barrage of stereotypes, oversimplified narratives, and a tendency to portray the US as either the ultimate savior of humanity or the root of all evil. It's as if Hollywood struggles to find a middle ground, often resorting to extremes to sensationalize and simplify complex issues for mass consumption. You’ll find depictions of Americans as either the loud, ignorant tourist or the heroic, gun-toting individual. So, while the American Dream is probably an oversimplification, I still believe Hollywood's greatest misrepresentation is in its portrayal of the American people. It's as though we are incapable of complex thought or emotional subtlety, something I find to be both insulting and untrue.

What movie felt like you were right there with the actors? I’m not sure I’ve ever felt ‘right there with the actors’ in a realistic sense—I’m very aware that I’m watching a constructed narrative, a fiction, a series of deliberate choices made by a director, a cinematographer, a whole crew. That said, I do, however, have films that create such robust worlds, so compelling in their verisimilitude, that I can lose myself in them, and for a couple of hours, the screen feels less like a barrier and more like a portal. One such movie is *The Insider* (1999), directed by Michael Mann. I have written about this before, and I recognize I am hardly alone in viewing this film with such reverence, but I return to it often. I watch it and try to understand how Mann’s team created such perfect artifice. It is, after all, a film about the art of artifice. Based on a true story, *The Insider* portrays the efforts of Jeffrey Wigand, a former tobacco executive (played impeccably by Russell Crowe), assisting a 60 Minutes producer, Lowell Bergman (Al Pacino), in exposing the corrupt practices of his former industry. The film is shot with such attention to detail, such precision in its composition, such commitment to an almost documentary realism, that you’re less watching a movie than eavesdropping on a series of crucial conversations. I would struggle to name a film I’ve watched that better captures the insidious nature of corporate power, the machinations of big business, the moral compromises individuals make in its service, and the slow, agonizing grind of fighting against it. Mann’s direction, his use of lighting, shadow, and colour, the performances, the sparse yet perfectly chosen musical score all combine to create a sense of unease, a constant thrum of tension, a sense that something terrible is about to happen. The film does all of this and does so whilst not sacrificing the human element to the story. At the core it’s a story about the power of friendship and the willingness to stand up for what is right. *The Insider* is a film that has stuck with me for years, not just as a cinematic achievement, but as a reminder of the importance of courage, conviction, and the battle for truth. It's not just a movie; it's a call to action, a whispered plea in the dark.

What are some dirty tactics used by fast food restaurants? Being a former fast food employee I’ve seen a fair share of things I'm not supposed to see. The industry thrives on a tightrope walk between profit margins and customer perception, and sometimes, the latter gets shortchanged. One of the most common practices, and this is across many chains, is the relentless pursuit of waste reduction, bordering on the absurd. Day-old fries magically re-emerge as "crispy" fries thanks to a stint in the fryer. Buns that have seen better days are cleverly concealed beneath a generous layer of sauce and toppings. Anything that can seemingly be resurrected is. Another tactic is the strategic placement of items on the menu, and promotional offers cleverly designed to lure you into buying more than you intended. Take the combo meal for instance. Seems like a good deal until you realize the individual items would have cost you less when purchased separately. Soda refills are another profit-driven strategy. Customers are sold a cup for a small price and then spend the next few hours consuming a bottomless pit of sugar and artificial sweeteners. This is often supplemented by limited-time offers, and bundle deals designed to shift customer’s attention to the product with the highest profit margin, even if it’s not the most popular or the most nutritious. One of the dirtier tactics I've come across is the under-the-table manipulation of portion sizes. A burger that used to be a certain size would inexplicably shrink over time. Those "value meals" that once offered decent servings would slowly diminish. This is usually done incrementally, to avoid customer outrage, but even a slight reduction in size can mean a significant increase in profit over a long period. It is a race to the bottom of the food chain. So, the next time you crave that late-night burger, remember that you may be getting more than than you bargained for.

How would you handle an employee who refuses to attend company parties? Company parties, eh? I’ve always found them to be an odd proposition. Forced merriment, arbitrary small talk, and the ever-looming threat of the boss’s misguided karaoke attempts always seemed a recipe for social awkwardness. I've observed many colleagues over the years. Some embrace these events with gusto, seeing them as an obligatory duty, an opportunity to climb the corporate ladder, or a chance to unwind – though "unwind" seems a tragically inaccurate description for getting hammered on cheap Pinot Grigio. Some just get hammered on the cheap Pinot Grigio. Then there are the introverts amongst us, the ones who skillfully maneuver through the office all year, hiding in plain sight and skillfully avoiding any social interaction whenever possible. They’re the ones who subtly disappear as soon as the clock strikes on Friday. The party is the inevitable reckoning of their reclusive existence. The ones who'd rather eat glass than stand and smile and nod at colleagues outside of work hours. Me? I've been all of these people over the years. It depends on the job, really. The first time I was forced to sing karaoke, I was mortified. It was a corporate retreat at some godforsaken resort with a tiny, cramped bar, serving watered down beer. I was still in my early 20s, and my boss cornered me and a few other new hires to “sing a song.” Let's just say I’ve never looked at Journey or "Don't Stop Believin'" in the same way. I was a wreck, a miserable, anxious shell of a human being. But on the other hand, later in life, I was the life of the party. Not because I suddenly loved socialising, but because I needed the job, and the ‘being the life of the party’ was a mandatory skill to learn. So, as an employer, how to handle an employee who’d rather skip these events? Well, it depends. If the employee is a consistent high performer, a valuable asset to the team? I'd probably let it slide. A low-key phone call, a reminder that company culture is important, and a gentle suggestion to make an appearance, even if it’s just for an hour, to show face. And if he/she shows up, buy him/her a drink. Beyond that? Leave them be. Some people are just wired differently, and forcing them to engage can do more harm than good. But, if that individual is a constant underperformer, a team player in name only? A gentle reminder of expectations, and a stronger encouragement to participate in activities that can help bring the team closer together is in order. Ultimately, you have to weigh the costs and benefits. Is this person’s absence truly detrimental, or is it just a minor inconvenience? And what's the cost of forcing someone to do something they clearly don't want to do? It's a delicate balance, navigating the murky waters of workplace social dynamics; after all nobody grows up dreaming of becoming the world's greatest office partier.

What is your biggest and weirdest pet peeve ever? This is a tricky one, as my pet peeves, the ones that truly grate on my nerves, are an eclectic mix of the mundane and the exceedingly odd. I've spent a considerable amount of time pondering this. The first that comes to mind is the persistent overuse of the word ‘literally’, completely detached from its actual meaning. I’m a man of the written word. Every sentence is a carefully constructed edifice, and to see that edifice demolished by the careless deployment of a word is both infuriating and heartbreaking. It’s right up there with incorrect grammar. Do not start a sentence with the coordinating conjunction ‘and’. Or so my English teacher would say. But let us not get bogged down on the mechanics of grammatical correctness. My pet peeve is in the use, or rather the misuse, of words. And no word is more misused than ‘literally’. The second is the overly enthusiastic use of the word ‘amazing’ to describe every single thing. This is an issue that most modern-minded individuals suffer with. A sunset in the Maldives? Absolutely breathtaking. The taste of a particularly good cup of coffee? Life-altering! It seems as if every aspect of mundane existence must be labeled ‘amazing’. The other peeve is the unrepentant belief in the world of astrology. I am not a skeptic of faith in general. I find it both fascinating and necessary for most people. But it's the complete lack of intellectual curiosity that is the true catalyst of unrest. No, your success, or failures, is not written in the stars. Not that I have anything against stars. They're far away, and they’re nice to look at. But I can not bring myself to accept the ridiculousness of many of the astrological assessments. I am particularly against individuals using it as an excuse for their actions. “I am a Sagittarius; therefore, I am predisposed to being a flake.” No, Karen. You are a flake because you are a flake.

What movies were so bad they actually made you angry, frustrated, or even caused you to walk out before the end? There's a difference between a bad movie and an *offensive* movie, something that genuinely gets under your skin and leaves you steaming. I’ve rarely walked out of a movie; usually, if I’ve committed to a flick, I'll see it through, even if it means enduring cinematic torture. A film rarely provokes any genuine anger in me. Usually, a bad movie is just a massive disappointment. I would only get angry if the badness was accompanied by perceived dishonesty or, worse, complete moral bankruptcy. However, I did once walk out of a movie. This happened around 2010. I was with a friend. We had gone to see *The Last Airbender* by M. Night Shyamalan. We waited with anticipation. *The Sixth Sense*, *Signs*, and even the underrated *Unbreakable* were movies I loved in my youth. My friend and I were not alone in waiting. We were children of the 90s. We were big fans of the cartoon, and the casting news was the cause of much debate amongst the fans. The hype was sky high. The lights went down. The film began. Five minutes in and I knew something was wrong. After 10–15 minutes, my friend and I were exchanging bewildered glances. It was clear Shyamalan had taken an entire dump on his source material. There was zero respect, zero understanding of the story. The dialogue was stilted, wooden, and borderline nonsensical. The characters, flat and uninteresting. The acting was shockingly inept. Everything was wrong. After an hour of slow motion, bad CGI, and an incomprehensible plot, my friend and I could take no more. We got up and left. It wasn't just bad; it was disrespectful. Disrespectful to the fans, to the source material, to the very concept of storytelling. We were both furious. I can only describe it as an affront to our intelligence and a betrayal of our expectations. We left the cinema and went to a bar to drown our sorrows with beers. I haven't set foot into a Shyamalan movie since then. It's a shame because I believed Shyamalan had a talent like no other. This movie, however, was a disaster. He should have known better. To me, this isn't just a bad movie; it is a genuine cinematic crime.

What are some plot holes in some of famous movies? The term "plot hole" has, in recent times, been a term far too loosely thrown around, particularly by fans of the comic book movie genre who appear eager to be the first to find fault with their favourite superhero/villain franchises. It all started with Jurassic Park (1993). The plot hole that everyone always mentions is the T-Rex chasing the jeep scene. Why didn't the T-Rex simply follow the jeep to the visitors' centre, wait until the people inside started filling up with food, then smash the glass windows and eat them? This isn't a plot hole, it’s a matter of suspense. At no point does Jurassic Park pretend that these dinosaurs exhibit the same behaviour as humans. What makes that scene work is not plot, but pure adrenaline. The plot hole is the ending. Everybody surviving on a helicopter knowing full well that the island is infested with dinosaurs who can fly, swim and burrow and yet somehow nobody ever goes back to do a proper investigation, or, for that matter, remove the menace? In fact, the film did not so subtly set up for a sequel. So, how about a sequel set about a year later, at a time when the dinosaurs have repopulated, or the various different breeds of dinosaurs have interbred, creating new hybrid dinosaurs? The first sequel was probably just a few years later. If the first movie was a commercial smash hit then why did the sequel seem to suck? Easy money. I always thought that plot hole in the James Bond movie Goldfinger was the most egregious. Bond is trapped in a plane held at gunpoint by Goldfinger's henchman, Oddjob. Goldfinger orders Oddjob to shoot Bond through the plane window. Oddjob objects, and refuses. This doesn't make any sense. He's just trying to execute an order. Oddjob's entire motivation depends on him executing Goldfinger's orders. He is a killer robot with the ability to kill with the most mundane of weapons. Bond at his most vulnerable. Why not just shoot Bond? The reason why is because it's a scene written to make Bond look good, not Goldfinger. Oddjob doesn't shoot Bond and instead, because of some contrivance, Bond escapes. The original Star Wars is filled with "plot holes". The Empire is fighting against the Rebel Alliance. The Rebel Alliance has the plans to the Death Star. The Death Star is a planet-sized battle station with the ability to destroy planets. The Empire's army is made up of Stormtroopers who can't shoot straight, have their bases easily infiltrated, and are all dressed in identical white uniforms. The Rebel Alliance's fighters somehow blow up the Death Star. The only reason the rebels got this lucky is because they were up against an army of incompetent Stormtroopers and also the Emperor himself.

What actors were supposed to be the next best thing in Hollywood but never made it? There are always a handful, aren't there? A few names spring to mind, instantly recognizable at one time, now seemingly vanished into the ether of "where are they now?" Take a look in the mirror, you'll see how easily fame can fade. Some of these actors, brimming with potential, burned bright but too quickly, consumed by the very fire that propelled them. You see them in the audition rooms, at acting schools, in the acting circles that populate your towns and cities. Some seemingly have the talent, the look, the charm, the charisma but, at some point they just faded away never to be seen again. Some actors, once the darlings of the industry, can't seem to maintain their luster. Others, like those shooting stars that streak across the night sky, blaze so brilliantly, it's hard to understand why their trajectory didn't lead to sustained stardom. I suppose a variety of factors could be blamed: poor choices, clashing personalities, the vagaries of public perception.  Consider the case of Freddie Prinze Jr. Handsome, charismatic, and with a string of successful teen comedies such as She’s All That and I Know What You Did Last Summer under his belt. He had the It factor. The kind you cannot fake. It seemed like he was destined to be a major player, a leading man of the era. But, after a few misfires and a shifting landscape of cinematic trends that started to be dominated by brooding superheroes and grim reboots, his star dimmed. There was also the matter of his personal life and how he was a bit too preoccupied in trying to have the life of a normal person and settling into the role of husband and father. This is no slight. It’s an understandable goal for any person but when you're trying to capture a piece of the Hollywood pie it can often be the death knell of a flourishing career. It's a matter of time and dedication. Or how about Leonardo DiCaprio prior to his success in the Titanic. Did you know that there was at one point heavy pressure placed upon the movie studio executives and other producers to recast him? Because it was felt that he was an acting oddity who would not have the requisite look to appeal to the wider audience. He was a risk. A gamble. And a damn successful one at that because DiCaprio played every factor to turn the tide in his favor. The ability to recognize your advantages and capitalize on them is a trait that cannot be understated. Or Matthew Lillard. He was in the teen slasher SCREAM and I had the idea that he would be an actor in great demand. He has done some work ever since but nothing substantial that would remind us of his early career prospects. So I'm not sure. Perhaps it is fate. Perhaps it is bad choices. Perhaps its is because acting is so damn arbitrary that it can never be pinned down.

What do fast food employees think of customers who come in frequently, say, multiple times a week or even daily? My only experience with the fast food industry was a short stint working at McDonald's during my college years, so take my anecdote for what it’s worth. Most of my coworkers were, to put it mildly, underwhelmed by the frequency of regulars. These were the folks who seemed to be perpetually in line, ordering the same thing every single time with a practiced ease that bordered on the uncanny. They knew the menu like the back of their hand and could recite their order with a speed that would make a seasoned auctioneer jealous: "Big Mac, no pickles, large fries, and a Diet Coke". And God forbid if you got it wrong. They would unleash a torrent of passive-aggressive complaints that could curdle milk. Then there were the truly dedicated ones, the ones who came in multiple times a day. You'd see them during the breakfast rush, again at lunch, and then - inexplicably - again during the dinner rush, seemingly immune to the very concept of cooking at home. We often wondered, more out of idle curiosity than genuine concern, what they did with their lives whilst consuming so many calories. Did they have a job? A family? Were they secretly secretly sponsored by the very company providing them their daily sustenance? Granted, the staff at McDonald's or any fast food restaurant are probably no different than any other worker. If an employee is confronted with a client who is an asshole, it's reasonable assumptions to think that employee most certainly doesn't like such an inconsiderate individual, however, if you’re polite, respectful, and easygoing, chances are employees will make your food more appealing. That's just how the world works. The most memorable customers would be the ones that would try to personalize the experience, the ones that would constantly test the boundaries of what was possible, the ones that would ask us "Is the ice cream machine working? Are the fries fresh?". We all knew, of course, they wanted a free something. You knew the type. Edit: And for the record. In my experience, the ice cream machines are ‘never’ working.

What is legal but ethically wrong? An interesting philosophical conundrum, that one. Let’s embark on a voyage of the morally grey, shall we? Many things fit this bill, wouldn't you agree? It’s all a matter of perspective. Take, for instance, the concept of "truth." In a court of law, it's illegal to lie under oath. Ethically, it's always reprehensible to deceive. But what about situations where telling the complete truth would cause significant harm? Is it ethically wrong to lie to save a life? Or, to put a less dramatic analogy, should a job applicant be upfront about their shortcomings during an interview? It's legal for a company to decline providing health insurance benefits to its workers. But is it ethically sound? Some would say yes, in a capitalistic framework, the company is acting in self-interest. Others would claim that the company bears a social responsibility to show concern for their employees. Or, there are those insufferable times when we simply *know* someone is lying. This is when the "white lie" becomes less about the act and more about the effect. It would be unethical to hurt the feelings of a friend or family member, so we tell the white lie. The law, of course, doesn’t have a category for such altruism. Or, consider the issue of exploitation. It's legal to hire workers at minimum wage, but is it ethical to pay them so little that they're struggling to survive? Is it ethical for a corporation to move its factory to a country with lax labor laws in order to take advantage of the lower cost of labor, even though it means that families are forced to work in deplorable conditions and are subjected to unsafe working environment? Legally, they’re within their rights. But morally? I think you can imagine the answer you'd get. The intersection of law and ethics is a murky one, a constant tension between rules and values. Sometimes, what is legal may indeed be ethically reprehensible, and vice versa. The world always seems to like making things difficult.

Which extremely surreal film would you consider to be worth watching? David Lynch's *Eraserhead* is my go-to answer. It's the kind of movie that stays with you long after the credits roll—or perhaps it never truly leaves. Shot in stark black and white, the film presents a disturbingly intimate and unsettling world. The visuals, a blend of industrial decay and nightmarish imagery, evoke a sense of creeping dread that burrows deep into your subconscious. The sound design, a cacophony of unsettling noises, further amplifies this effect. The narrative, or lack thereof, is as enigmatic as it is disturbing. A man, Henry Spencer, navigates an existence of squalor, parenthood, and profound alienation. He is visited with a deformed child, with the constant wails and disturbing noises contributing to his ever increasing anguish. His relationships are as abnormal and unsettling as his environment. There are no easy answers, no neatly packaged morals. It’s a descent into the depths of human experience and the film leaves you to grapple with its meaning. *Eraserhead* isn't just a film; it's an experience. It's not for everyone. It is defiantly not for the casual viewer. If you're looking for a clear plot or straightforward resolution, you'll be disappointed. If you're open to exploring the darkest corners of the human psyche and willing to be profoundly unsettled, then, by all means, watch it. Consider yourself warned though. It’s the sort of movie that can warp your perception of reality, making you question everything you thought you knew about film, life, and perhaps even yourself. It's a masterpiece of the bizarre, a cinematic poem of human fears, and a must-see for anyone willing to embrace the uncanny. The film is a powerful and unforgettable viewing experience, a true landmark of surreal cinema.

Without saying their name, who is your favorite fictional character? This is tough. I have so many. I'm a sucker for the anti-hero. The complicated character who does bad things but for reasons you, kinda, begrudgingly understand. I’m not going to be original when I say it's The Joker. Not the Heath Ledger version. Not the Joaquin Phoenix version. All of them are brilliant. I love the comic book version. The idea is not the character himself but the circumstances that led him to be the way he is. A product of the worst possible things that can happen to a person. If I were to be more original I would have said Walter White from Breaking Bad, another of my favorite anti-heroes. But this got me thinking. It's the circumstances that made them the way they are. Nobody is born bad. They are made that way. I thought of other characters that fit this criteria. Hannibal Lecter, Nurse Ratched, Darth Vader. So many to choose from. But I'm boring. I’ll stick with The Joker. The character is a blank canvas. No history. No name. Nobody knows what he was like before he became The Joker. Is he insane or is it some kind of performance? Is he evil? Yes. Is he evil? I never know who he is and that’s what makes him interesting. The Joker is terrifying because he is a symbol of absolute chaos. Maybe I just really like chaos.

Would Hollywood actor Brad Pitt have made it in old or classic Hollywood back in the day? Brad Pitt’s chiseled physique and undeniable charisma definitely would have made a splash in the Golden Age of Hollywood, though perhaps for different reasons. Back then, leading men were often groomed, quite literally, to fit a certain mold of refined masculinity not unlike the old school male beauty pageant contestants of yesteryear. We're talking immaculate hair, tailored suits, and an air of sophistication that screamed "wealthy socialite." Pitt, while possessing those qualities, also carries a certain raw, almost rebellious energy that might have clashed with the studio system's rigid control. He just seems like someone who’d constantly butt heads with the studio heads. He's also a pretty good actor. If you're giving someone the role, you should give it to someone with the ability to act. He’d probably have been fine with the constant media attention from fans. In Classic Hollywood being a movie star sometimes meant you'd get mobbed by hundreds of screaming fans, some of whom were going to pull off your cufflinks. Pitt, however, possesses a modern star power that transcends mere good looks. He's got acting chops, and a certain je ne sais quoi. Ultimately, Pitt's success in classic Hollywood would have likely depended on his ability to navigate the studio system and adapt to the era's constraints. Could you see him playing a suave, yet stoic, detective in a noir film, or perhaps a dashing, yet ultimately tragic, romantic hero in a sweeping historical drama? I bet you could.

What was the first thing you saw, heard or discovered that made you feel old? The first thing that comes to mind is when I realised I was no longer interested in popular music. Growing up, I was a fanatic of bands like Nirvana, Oasis, and Blur. I memorized the lyrics to every song, bought every album, stayed up late to watch the music videos on MTV, and, of course, dressed the part. I recall when I was a teenager, I attended a gig with a friend and thought "this is it, this is the height of cool." When the lights came up at the end of the gig, my ears were ringing with the sound of feedback. I was ecstatic. I remember thinking that a musician had actually created an orchestra of noise and it was beautiful. It wasn't long ago that those bands were still played on the radio. I was in my early 20s when a friend showed me some new music. I remember taking one listen to their music and thinking, "this is just noise." I felt a visceral reaction, like my ears were rebelling. I can't remember what it was exactly but it was a sound that was obviously produced by computers. I remember saying to myself "this is not music," and that was the moment I felt old. I was being the grumpy older generation, complaining about the changing times. I had become my parents. I was no longer in touch with what the youth of today found cool nor did I want to be. I feel that this experience is similar to the experience our parents had when we were being rebellious teenagers blasting heavy rock music, listening to bands like Led Zeppelin and The Rolling Stones while they were shaking their heads and complaining "that's not music." Now I am on the other side of the generational gap, with the same feelings. I have not been able to keep up with the changes in music in the past decade. I still find the music of the 90s and early 2000s to be relatable. Whenever I hear music from the past fifty years, I remember the memories associated with those songs. I can't say the same for more recent music. Now that I am older, I find myself drawn to older music and I now understand why my parents did. I can say that on that day, I became the man I used to ridicule.

Do you ever regret having or do you regret not having kids? This is a tough one. Being a cinema usher, a career path hardly conducive to family life, always gave me a front-row seat to the myriad lives unfolding before me. I saw the weary parents lugging toddlers and their assorted paraphernalia, their faces etched with a fatigue that only the truly sleep-deprived understand. Then there were the boisterous families, kids hopped up on sugar and the parents trying to maintain a semblance of control. Yet, I also keenly observed the couples, hand-in-hand, relishing a stolen moment away from the daily grind, their gaze fixed on the screen. Having kids is a monumental decision. There’s no taking it back. It’s a gamble, a roll of the dice, a leap into the unknown. And for what? For love? For legacy? For purpose? For me, it was almost always a ‘no’. I never had that burning biological imperative, that primal urge to propagate the species. I enjoyed my freedom, my spontaneity, my ability to make decisions based solely on my own desires.

What's the most ruthless thing a new boss has done to show he/she is in charge? My initial job after graduating college was at a major financial institution, a rather soulless outfit in my estimation. My immediate supervisor was a decent fellow. He had a good heart, was a good teacher and a genuinely considerate person. However, upper management, which was comprised of the usual collection of entitled, Harvard Business School graduates from privileged backgrounds, was a different kettle of fish entirely. Our department was overseen by a ruthless, calculating woman who had no regard for the feelings or career prospects of the staff. Her primary objective was to climb the corporate ladder, regardless of the cost to others. One morning, she called a meeting, ostensibly to discuss a new initiative. In reality, it was a power play. She singled out a mid-level manager who, frankly, was a little long in the tooth and hadn't been as effective as the other more ambitious and younger managers. The target of her ire had been with the company for over 20 years. He was well-liked, competent enough, and knew the ins and outs of the business. The new VP opened the meeting by praising the department’s recent success. Then, seemingly out of nowhere, she began deconstructing one of the manager's reports. It became apparent after a few minutes that she was not only criticizing his work but also mocking his experience in the business. She claimed he was out of step and didn't possess the skills needed to succeed. And that the company had no use for employees like him. There was, to reiterate, no reason for her to be singling out anyone as the department was performing well and to the best of my knowledge, there had been no major complaints. There were no formal complaints against him. He'd always performed his duties amicably. She didn’t stop with her verbal assault. It was, to borrow a term from the world of professional wrestling, a full-blown heel turn. She spent the next hour completely eviscerating the man’s career at the company. She questioned his judgment, his ability. She even went so far as to belittle his intelligence. The man, understandably, was visibly shaken, but he remained composed, answering her questions, trying to defend himself. Then, she looked at him and, with an icy smile, announced that a new manager had been selected to oversee his department and that he was to be reassigned to a new role. It quickly became apparent he would be working under his peers, under a new set of underlings and that he was going to take on additional workload. The new role was a dead-end one and it would effectively end his career at the financial institution. The entire scene was meticulously crafted to display the VP's power. It was a brutal, public display of authority, a ruthless demonstration of her willingness to sacrifice anyone to achieve her personal goals. And sadly, it worked.

If you could choose only one font which one would it be and why? This is a thought experiment with no right answers. So, I’d choose Times New Roman. Not because it’s the most aesthetically pleasing font, it's not, or the best, but because it's the most ubiquitous. I write in many different fonts out of personal preference. But in the end I always resort to Times New Roman. One could say it’s the most boring font. But its familiarity makes it the most reader-friendly. Its basic serifs and well-defined letterforms allow for easy readability across various mediums; from the printed page to the digital screen. It's a workhorse, a dependable choice. It's the default for a reason. Think about it. If I had to write a letter, a business document, or an essay that will be read across a wide range of devices, I'd choose Times New Roman. It offers a uniform visual experience and is less likely to cause text rendering issues or font substitution problems. It doesn't scream for attention, it simply gets the job done efficiently and effectively. It's the dependable Ford pickup truck of the font world. It may not be fancy or beautiful, but it will always start, always perform as expected, and won't let you down. It’s a safe choice, a pragmatic choice. If I was shipwrecked and only had the font of Times New Roman to save me, I would be alright.

What are the things no one tells you about living alone? Many people are in such a rush to move out of their parents’ homes and ‘live their best lives,’ that they don’t take the time to investigate the realities of independence. They see Instagram, TikTok and social media in general as the gospel truth of this seemingly great life. All the parties, the freedom, the sex, the glamorous apartments, travelling the world. The truth is, living alone is an exercise in extreme discipline. No one is there to kick you out of bed. No one is there to make you dinner. The dishes will not wash themselves. The laundry will not fold itself. These are the most obvious points but they're the ones which many first timers overlook. Few people understand the monotony of living alone. You’re alone. All of the time. Your friends and family will not visit every day or even every week. You’ll find yourself in a perpetual cycle of eating alone, watching alone, working alone. You will have to actively seek out people, activities, outings to combat this; not just passively wait by the phone for someone to call or text. There’s also the matter of money, if the bills aren't paid on time you have little room to maneuver. Rent is set, utilities are set, and groceries and fuel are set. Unless you have vast reserves, that leaves little to play with for leisure. This, of course, is what leads young people to think that they might be better off staying home to save money. It’s a difficult balance, between needing to break free from the nest combined with facing the harsh economic realities of independence. I understand the need to move out. Being out on your own, is the closest thing to true freedom available. The loneliness and economics are just some of the things you have to be prepared for. Then there’s the things nobody tells you about the apartment itself; the creaks, the flickering lights, the mysterious sounds from the neighbors and the sheer loneliness which overwhelms anyone and everyone at times whether they are mentally robust or not. The first night in a new home is a true test. I remember my first night. I was filled with the most peculiar combination of ecstasy and dread. Ecstasy at the freedom. Dread at the unknown. Those things are the hardest to get through.

Are there parents who regret having mixed-race children? Regret is a particularly loaded word. I am absolutely certain that there are parents, somewhere, who experience regret, not just in having mixed-race children, but with children in general. I don’t believe that they are regretting the existence of their offspring, but that they regret the responsibility, the challenges, the sacrifices, the sheer, unrelenting exhaustion of parenthood. The demands are extraordinary. These are the circumstances of parenthood, not exclusively of raising a mixed-race child. I’m willing to bet that an overwhelming amount of the parents of mixed-race children, of any background, would claim that the experience has been overwhelmingly positive. But no doubt there are those who harbor some resentment. Having a child is life-altering. The vast majority of us get over that, or at least accommodate ourselves to the radical changes to our lifestyles. But, there are the outliers, who struggle to adapt. As someone who has never had children I am simply speculating here and I can only guess at the intense emotions involved. But I daresay it is not exclusive to mixed-race families. Every year there is a new study emerging that confirms how race is so overwhelmingly and deeply divisive in American society. We are still arguing about skin color more than 150 years after the end of the Civil War and 60+ year since the Civil Rights Act. The fact is some people are just flat outright racist or hold deep set prejudices. It really is that simple. Racism is not a difficult thing to understand. They might have had a change of heart. They might go on to have their own families and then change their mind. They may have had an abusive childhood and then struggle to become good parents. I believe that many people believe that if they are racist, it is okay if they are "good" racists. They make no apologies for using racial or ethnic slurs but they like to claim that they are against violence and racial profiling and they make certain that they are treating everyone equally. Of course for them that means that they are nice towards white people. People in general also do not apply the lessons that they learn about the world to themselves. They believe that they are special and that the lessons being imparted from history apply to everyone else but them. I imagine most of the "regret" is likely to do with external factors. Some may have been from families who were not welcoming, or from societies who had made their feelings quite clear. Perhaps they struggled to raise their child/children in a safe environment without experiencing the constant everyday overt or coded racism. Having a mixed-race child may bring its extra problems. I am very interested in the subject and am eager to know what people have to say, and will read through all answers.

What is an example of an album that, in your opinion, was ruined by the producer and/or the production? I'd have to say Metallica's *...And Justice for All* (1988). The band, riding the success of *Master of Puppets*, was at the height of its powers, capable of churning out complex, progressive thrash metal that fused technical proficiency with raw energy. This should have been a monumental album, a definitive statement of their artistry. Instead, what we got was a sonic catastrophe. The primary culprit? The infamous, almost nonexistent bass guitar.  Jason Newsted, the newly-minted bassist who replaced Cliff Burton after his tragic death, poured his heart and soul into the album, as did the rest of the band, but the production—or, more accurately, the *lack* thereof—rendered his efforts virtually inaudible. It's a decision that baffles, frustrates, and infuriates fans to this day. It's as if someone decided to remove a crucial ingredient from a masterpiece, leaving the final product hollow, unbalanced, and fundamentally flawed and this, to put it mildly, is a disaster. The blame is often laid at the feet of Lars Ulrich, who along with James Hetfield co-produced the album. There are many speculations about this decision ranging from simply disliking bass in general to a childish ‘hazing ritual’ of sorts for the new bassist however that is not my point of concern. A guitar solo is a great moment in a song. A bass solo in the context of music is a rarer occasion but still a great moment, and the music could shine here. But after the album was ‘released,’ the music essentially became a cacophony of clanging guitars and drums with minimal audible bass (which is, of course, paramount to the metal genre). This wasn't simply a matter of a subtle mix or a preference for a particular instrument. The bass was essentially *removed* from the mix, leading to a jarring and alienating listening experience with what could’ve become an epoch-defining album. It wasn’t the result of technical limitations or some kind of experimental vision. It was, quite simply, a major oversight, a catastrophic decision that robbed *...And Justice for All* of its full potential. The music, once bursting with life, feels lifeless and thin. A work of art, tragically compromised.

What screams "I make terrible financial decisions!"? Buying a sports car. Or a boat. Or a McMansion. Or all three. It's a cliché at this point, but clichés are often rooted in truth. I'm not immune. I make my share of financially unsound choices. One time, I bought a limited-edition, imported, overpriced bottle of whiskey from a store clerk who looked like he was still in high school. I have no idea why. It's still languishing unopened in my cupboard. My more sensible friends shake their heads, but what can I say? I'm a sucker for the allure of the extravagant. Another financial misstep? Impulse purchases on Amazon at 2 a.m. fueled by a cocktail of insomnia and the dopamine rush that comes with "one-click" buying. The next morning I'm left wondering what possessed me to purchase a life-sized cardboard cutout of a celebrity. It was a regrettable decision, but also kind of awesome in a profoundly sad way. I've considered selling it, but the thing has a certain nostalgic appeal. Some would say that buying physical media – vinyl records, Blu-rays, and the like – is another financial folly. Digital streaming services are cheaper and more convenient, after all.

Can you name an actor who was never a good actor but became one? Nicolas Cage, probably. He used to be such a terrible, over-the-top, coked-up caricature of a human being in his early movies. Then, as years went by he sort of became watchable, even good, and then, well, maybe he was still a caricature but at the same time you knew what he was doing and he looked like he was enjoying himself. You could tell he was having fun whilst making terrible movies. Sometimes fun comes out on the screen and people get sucked in. In his films, you had this really bad guy, this really, really bad guy but he wouldn't kill people. He would just make them sad, like he was getting off on the misery of others instead of doing anything drastic. But later on, he just kept making terrible films year after year. He never became a good actor, he just got more successful at being Nicolas Cage. I actually sort of admire that. He just does what he does, and if people like it, they like it. If they don't, they don't. He never seemed particularly bothered. I think that's an admirable way to go about things. I wouldn't say he’s the best actor ever, but he is certainly one of the most interesting. Besides, who really cares if somebody is objectively "good" or not? If they bring you joy, that's all that matters. Sure, there are the greats, the Daniel Day-Lewises, the Marlon Brandos, the Meryl Streeps, the Cate Blanchetts. These are obviously great, but they're not necessarily the most exciting or fun to watch. I can appreciate their craft but don't particularly care about their movie choices. Give me Cage chewing the scenery any day of the week.

What television shows started strong only to become unwatchable later? Television shows, like life, rarely sustain their initial momentum; the precipice for spectacular implosion is always just ahead. The allure of a captivating pilot is often squandered by a combination of writer's block, executive meddling, and a general lack of foresight. One such example, which still smarts to this day, is the trajectory of *Lost*. The first few seasons were a masterpiece of mystery, character development, and suspense. Every week, a new puzzle piece was slid into place, and the audience was enthralled with the various plots, characters, and how they intertwined. Then the writers, in their infinite wisdom decided to overplay their hand, to keep the mystery going at all costs. Answers were withheld. Instead of a satisfying resolution, *Lost* culminated in a series of increasingly unsatisfying reveals and bizarre plot twists, and a finale that generated more befuddlement and outrage than closure. The show seemingly evaporated into a haze of convoluted mythology. The brilliance that was once there was replaced by an impenetrable thicket of nonsense. One also has to consider, once a show becomes popular and earns a massive fan base, the need to stay on the air. *Dexter*, for example, started off brilliantly in the early seasons. A fascinating premise, a complex protagonist, and a supporting cast of characters who were just as compelling. However, as the seasons wore on, the writing started to suffer. The plots grew repetitive, the villains less memorable and the show seemed content to coast on its existing success, not wanting to give the show a decisive ending. There was no longer a drive to be *good*, but rather, to remain. The later seasons were a pale imitation of the early brilliance. The show stumbled towards a conclusion that felt both rushed and underwhelming, with predictable plotlines. It's a perfect illustration of a show losing its way in the pursuit of longevity. Some shows lose their way due to cast departures, writers’ strikes etc. Still, television viewing is a risky business. You may invest hours and hours on a weekly basis, only to feel betrayed by the ultimate destination.

What's the worst experience you've had with telling someone you had feelings for them? This one hits hard, because it’s still raw, but I'll share. Back in college, there was this girl—let's call her Sarah—with whom I was utterly smitten. We were in the same film studies class and bonded over a shared disdain for Michael Bay movies as well as a secret affinity for the low-budget, cult-classic horror flicks of the 70s and 80s. Sarah was everything I wasn’t: confident, witty, and possessed of a devilish sense of humor that could disarm anyone. It was a slow burn; a series of furtive glances across the lecture room, mumbled conversations over coffee, and the shared experience of cringing through the required viewing of a particularly pretentious French New Wave film. I'd thought I'd cultivated enough courage over the semester, so I decided, fueled by liquid courage and a healthy dose of youthful delusion, I was going to lay bare my feelings for her. I crafted the perfect plan. I remember it was late at night, a Friday. I'd invite her over to my dormitory to "watch movies". I picked out some obscure films, and planned the perfect setting to "accidentally" reveal my affection. The night came, and thankfully, she agreed. The movies were a disaster of awkward silences and nervous laughter. Finally, as the credits of *Slaughterhouse* began to roll, I decided it was time to act. I cleared my throat, and tried to sound relaxed. "Sarah," I began, forcing my eyes to meet hers, "I, uh, I like you." She gave me this look—a mix of surprise and confusion—and then after what seemed like an eternity, let out the most delicate laugh. I was terrified. My heart hammered against my ribs like a trapped bird. Then came the words that still echo in my head. ‘You’re a really nice, really nice guy, but you’re kinda…not my type.’ And that, my friends, was that. I tried to play it cool, but it was an utter catastrophe. We finished the night in silence. The next morning, I learned her phone number had been changed. She had blocked my number. To this day, I can't listen to a Van Morrison or The Smiths song without reliving that agonizing night.

Which character did you view totally differently as a child vs. as an adult? There are many characters I saw with different eyes growing up versus now, but the one that truly stands out is the Wicked Witch of the West from *The Wizard of Oz*. As a child, she was the quintessential villain: green-skinned, cackling, and with a penchant for threatening Dorothy and her friends. She was the embodiment of pure, unadulterated evil, solely existing to terrorize and foil the heroes. Her motivations were simple, her actions cartoonishly wicked. The only thing I knew was that I was supposed to hate her, and I did, with every fiber of my being. The very thought of her was a source of nightly nightmares for me. It wasn't hard to see her as a truly despicable character. An adult perspective, however, adds layers of complexity to the character. Her menacing presence and the sheer power she wielded still remain, of course. But now, one realizes that she isn’t just a mustache-twirling villain, she is a woman protecting what’s hers. The ruby slippers, the symbols of power, were hers to begin with. Dorothy's arrival, her unforeseen presence, and her unforeseen, accidental act set the stage for everything that transpired. She was not inherently evil, but rather reactive. She was a businesswoman, a power broker, and a victim of circumstance whose kingdom was suddenly invaded by a strange girl from Kansas and, thus had to make a calculated move to defend what she perceived as rightfully hers.

What’s your relationship with alcohol? I'm not one for strong drinks. It's not that I eschew alcohol altogether. I'll take a glass of wine with dinner, a beer on a hot day, or a cocktail at a party, but I don't particularly crave it and I certainly don't need it. My relationship with alcohol is more akin to a polite acquaintance than a close friend. I grew up in a household where both parents enjoyed a casual drink, but there was never any excess or abuse. It was simply a part of life, a way to unwind at the end of a long day or to celebrate a special occasion. This instilled in me a healthy respect for alcohol, understanding it as a social lubricant, a source of potential enjoyment, but never a necessity. I've seen the damage alcohol can inflict; the lives ruined, the relationships destroyed, the health jeopardized. It's a powerful substance, and it needs to be treated with caution. Perhaps because of this observation, and growing up in the time I did, I've always been very cautious, but in my opinion, not overly so. I'm grateful for the ability to enjoy alcohol in moderation, to appreciate its flavor and its accompanying social aspects; but I'm even more grateful for the lack of any real attachment. It's a comfortable and, ultimately, unremarkable place to be.

What turns people off about Quora? I’ve used Quora a few times. I've stopped. Here are my observations. Firstly, there's a preponderance of the "expert," the person who thinks they know everything. Whether they are doctors, lawyers, or self-proclaimed CEOs, they all seem to be experts, ready to dispense profound advice on everything from optimal parenting to the nuanced philosophy of Nietzsche. This would be fine if these individuals occasionally acknowledged their limitations or the grey areas of the topics they discuss. But many do not. Instead, they project an aura of unshakeable certainty, which can easily be off-putting to anyone who appreciates nuance and skepticism. Secondly, there is a severe problem of vanity. Many users seem more interested in showcasing themselves than genuinely contributing to a meaningful discussion. A question such as the one above morphs into a vehicle for self-promotion, where people use their answers to subtly (or not so subtly) insert anecdotes about their accomplishments, expertise, or enlightened perspectives. This is particularly apparent when personal stories are shoehorned into answers that have little to do with the original question. The worst of the lot are the frequent links to personal blogs, YouTube channels, or self-published books. It is very hard to ascertain whether the content even has any relevance to the original question or it has just been thrown in there out of pure self-interest. I used to believe that free content was the panacea for the internet. It might be, but by using Quora I’ve come to understand that free content also attracts narcissists, people who are willing to use others for their personal gain. Finally, the platform itself does not adequately police the quality of discourse. It’s relatively easy for inaccurate information or outright propaganda to spread like wildfire. Trolls and those with axes to grind can, and do, hijack threads, turning potentially informative discussions into flame wars. The downvote function is often misused, not as a measure of informational accuracy, but as a means to punish views the user doesn’t agree with. I can see why Quora is popular, but it's a bit too much for me to stomach.

Do biracial people ever pick their white side and identify as white? This is a complicated question, and one that I'm not equipped to give a definite answer to, but I shall try. "White" is a socially constructed label, not a biological one, and the concept of "race" itself is a historical and political artifact. People's self-identification is a fluid and complex thing. Consider this: I am of mixed Caribbean heritage, and my skin is a tanned colour. I am often mistaken for either Latino or Indian. I don't mind at all, but I also find it strange because in the old days, my parents made a habit out of telling me of my race. I am Black. Some of my friends have one parent who's Black and one parent who's White, but they identify as Black. Others may identify more with their white heritage because they have a closer connection to that side of their family, or maybe because socially they move through the world in ways that mean they feel more connected to the culture of whiteness and, perhaps, are treated with more privilege because of their phenotype. Or maybe they just like the way it looks or sound. There is no simple answer; everyone is different, and the spectrum of how people experience race and identity can vary greatly. We are not even beginning to scratch the surface of the various intersectionalities, nuances, and complexities of racial identity.

What actor’s acting style has aged the worst? I'll go with Al Pacino. There’s no doubt that the man is a legend. He gave us some unforgettable performances in Godfather I & II, Dog Day Afternoon, Serpico, Scarface, Heat, The Insider, and Devil’s Advocate. He showed the world that there was a world of nuance in the role of a gangster, a cop, a lawyer, a whistleblower etc. He made the world stand still with his explosive charisma. He redefined what it meant to be a tough guy. My God that iconic scene in Godfather II where he gives his brother the kiss of death is one of the greatest acting performances in cinematic history. However, I would have to say that his acting style has aged considerably. The man is now a caricature of himself. He shouts and screams in almost every scene, his gestures are overly dramatic, his eye movements are excessively frantic. It's as if he believes that if he's loud and dramatic for 100% of the time the audience would think he's acting. This style of acting just doesn't work in modern filmmaking. It's okay if you're reading Shakespeare but modern film calls for something more nuanced, something more subtle, like acting. The worst example I can think of is his performance in the 2012 film Jack and Jill. His performance was so cringe worthy, so over-the-top that I refused to watch any more credits. Whenever I would see trailers of his movies, the only thing that prevented from switching the channel was the hope that the man had given up the overacting shtick and would finally deliver. He hasn't. His acting style is like listening to a screeching violin being played at max volume by a man who is not even trying.

Who are the most uncomfortable movie characters depicting the UK that you’ve ever seen? There are so many options to choose from but I'm going to go with the more recent examples. In the Marvel Cinematic Universe, Daniel Brühl who is of German descent, plays Baron Zemo in Captain America: Civil War (2016) and The Falcon and the Winter Soldier (2021) - whose character is a citizen of the fictional nation of Sokovia. In the former, he is shown torturing a former British soldier, played by Martin Freeman, to gather intel so as to frame the Winter Soldier for the bombing of the UN. He does so with a ridiculous, cartoonishly bad British accent which can only be described as borderline offensive. It's not just that the accent is bad. The whole idea that because he's trying to impersonate somebody, he's able to come up with a Brit-ish accent simply by copying it. This smacks of laziness. And by the time, he appears in The Falcon and the Winter Soldier, the accent hasn't improved at all, if anything it has gotten far worse. This wouldn't be so bad except for the fact that you can't go online without seeing multiple articles, videos and YouTube clips praising Brühl's acting ability and how he is the ‘underrated’ actor in the MCU. You can’t fault someone for their acting ability, sometimes even if they are very bad at what they are doing. Perhaps this is a case of the actor putting in a lot of effort? I don’t know. I've seen Daniel Brühl in other movies with only minor roles, and he's actually good and he can portray other accents. My only conclusion would be that it's a matter of directors and screenwriters who just did not care about the authenticity of the accent. The same can be said for the character of Agatha Harkness played by Kathryn Hahn in the Marvel Cinematic Universe show, WandaVision. Hahn is an American actress, the accent she does in the show is a broad, almost caricature English accent. It's not just that her accent is bad, but it's the characterization, in that they are playing up all sorts of eccentric elements that just don't exist. The casting departments seem to think that an English person is an automatic villain. And that any British character can't talk without employing dark humour and using sarcasm as a weapon. It's exhausting. Both of their performances are what I would describe as uncomfortable for any Brit. It's insulting.

Who’s your favorite redhead? For me, it’s a tie between the two redheaded Irishmen: Domhnall Gleeson and Michael Fassbender. They're both superb actors and are extremely versatile; they are both capable of playing a whole spectrum of characters ranging from comedic to dramatic to psychotic. But in terms of sheer ‘sex appeal’, it’s Fassbender hands down. If you ask most women, they'd probably say the same. He can brood and smolder better than most anyone out there. And it also helps that he doesn't seem to take himself too seriously. He has a certain boyish charm and wit. Look at his turn as Magneto in the X-Men movies. He is one of the most charismatic and iconic villains in the whole of comic book film adaptations. Domhnall Gleeson has a sort of friendly, nerdy, affable charm. It's easy to imagine him as your friend’s slightly awkward, unassuming brother and then also, it is equally easy to imagine him as the next Bond villain, slowly and methodically torturing Bond whilst also keeping his charm about him. Both of these actors have great range. I like that about them. Their ability to transform themselves and take on completely different roles. Sometimes I cannot believe it’s the same actor. Who else? Is there any other redhead who is currently popular? I am not familiar with the current crop of young actors. I’m not a connoisseur of pop culture. I’m more of a ‘classic’ kind of guy. I guess you could say I am old school in that respect. When a classic movie comes on television I'd pick it over some new Marvel Cinematic Universe movie, any day of the week. I suppose that could be a subject for a wholly other post: “Why I am sick and tired of the Marvel Cinematic Universe and why I prefer the movies of the 70s and the 80s”. I have thought about that. When you look at actors from that era, the vast majority of them are really superb. Whereas a large number of today’s actors are, how to put it… Well, I believe that a lot of today’s male actors are not ‘men’ at all. They are more like ‘boys’. And, quite frankly, for all of the supposed emancipation and liberation of women, they are not what a lot of women desire. They are not who many women want. Not the ones I know, anyway. You see it in most of the movies today. The male leads tend to be whiny, self-absorbed, fragile characters who are completely reliant on the female leads to make the tough decisions and be the ones with all the backbone. It's a role reversal.

What are the cleverest scams you have come across? I’ve come across a few, but the one that always sticks with me involves the diamond trade. It happened many years ago, back when I was just a fresh-faced grad, eager to make my mark on the world. I was in a bustling marketplace in Bangkok, a place teeming with exotic goods, hustlers and the promise of a quick buck. I remember being approached by a well-dressed gentleman, speaking in a convincing British accent. He introduced himself as a diamond broker, selling stones at a ‘once-in-a-lifetime’ price. He gestured towards a small, velvet case - “A family inheritance, you see, selling for far less than they’re worth due to circumstances.” He then proceeded to flash some certificates, showing that they were real, which I later learned could be easily faked. The stones themselves were flawless, sparkling under the harsh Thai sun. He said they were worth a fortune, and while I’d never been much of an expert in the gemological arts, the logic was sound: buy low, sell high. I lacked the funds, but he said that he wants to make me his partner; I'd put up a little bit of money, and he'd work with the diamonds. What could go wrong? I'm an idiot. I bit hook, line, and sinker, and put in a large sum of money that I borrowed from my friend. I never saw the man again, let alone the diamonds. It was embarrassing. The scam was simple but effective. He targeted people who were vulnerable and easily swayed. My own naiveté and greed made me an easy mark. Then, there was the case of the Nigerian prince. Again, this one relied on human greed. The scammer would send out emails, promising massive rewards for helping him transfer money out of his country. The key factor was the outlandishness of the claim; to a degree with the diamond scam, a person can claim to be a diamond merchant so as to con victims, but only a fool would believe that a prince would give you a massive sum of money. The emails didn’t even bother trying to be believable. They were riddled with grammatical errors and the requests were absurd. But people still fell for it, because the amount of money on offer triggered a deep-seated element of wanting something for nothing. People get this thing in their brains, something like a compulsion, where they think, “Well, this is ridiculous, but what if it’s true?” and their minds just shut off. The scammers knew this, and they relied on it. They were not trying to fool everyone. They were simply screening all potential victims looking for people with a certain kind of mindset. The cleverness of both scams, and the numerous others I could mention, wasn’t in the ingenuity of their design, but in the exploitation of human nature.

What is the weirdest thing you've ever witnessed a parent do? Growing up, I always thought my parents were fairly normal, but looking back, there were definitely some eccentricities. However, the weirdest thing I ever personally witnessed a parent do didn't involve my own. My friend, let’s call him David, lived in a house that, to a wide-eyed kid, seemed like a genuine haunted mansion. It was an old, creaky Victorian, with gables and turrets and a looming, ivy-covered facade. David's parents were, to put it mildly, unconventional. His father, a portly man with an impressive mustache and a penchant for tweed, collected antique clocks and had a habit of wandering around the house in a dressing gown, muttering about the "unseen forces" that supposedly governed the universe. His mother, a gaunt woman with long, silver hair, was a practicing Wiccan who frequently hosted ritualistic gatherings in their dimly lit living room. The weirdest thing I ever saw was during a particularly hot summer afternoon. David and I, bored with the usual childhood pursuits, were exploring the labyrinthine basement, which was filled with cobwebs, dusty furniture, and the general detritus of decades of neglect. We stumbled upon a small, locked room we'd never seen before. Curiosity piqued, we started to investigate. After a few minutes of trying, we finally managed to pick the lock and open the door. Inside, there was nothing but a grand piano, covered in a thick layer of dust, facing a mirror. David’s mother entered the room. She stood motionless for several minutes, holding a dead, black cat. She then proceeded to place the cat on the piano, positioned the mirror so that the cat could see its own reflection, and began to play a mournful melody, her eyes closed, her face streaked with tears. David and I quietly backed away, leaving her to her bizarre, grief-stricken ritual. We never spoke about it afterward, neither to each other nor to anyone else. We just filed it away in the category of ‘things best left unexplained,’ alongside the mysterious noises, the flickering lights, and the general feeling that something was always watching us from the shadows.

What is one thing that all men hate? The most universally loathed thing amongst men? Waiting. Not waiting in line for a movie, not waiting for a delayed train, not waiting for a doctor, not waiting for anything that's outside of one's control. Men hate waiting on *things* that are within their control. If a man is assembling something, be it furniture or a computer, and a crucial screw is missing? Agony. If a man is cooking something on the stove and he's run out of an ingredient? Catastrophe. If a man is attempting to do any work, be it physical, mental, or creative, and a crucial tool has gone missing? He will have to stop everything and dedicate his undivided attention to finding this thing. This is a truth as old as time: a man is only as functional as the tools he has at his disposal. One could be the most skilled carpenter in South America, but if he is without his prized saw, then all he is is a man with strong arms and a pile of wood.

What was the "I'm done" moment in your last relationship? I've been pondering this question for a while. I suppose the "I'm done" moment in my last relationship wasn't a singular incident, rather a slow, insidious erosion of the foundation upon which the relationship was built. It’s like those old, grainy, black and white movies where the lovers are running towards the train tracks, only the train is never coming. The moment wasn’t a dramatic explosion of fury or a tearful confession, but a quiet realization that the train wouldn’t come. We had a tendency of talking over one another, and for the longest of times I always interpreted this as a sign of our excitement in each other’s company. A shared enthusiasm. But then the scales fell from my eyes. We weren’t talking over each other due to excitement, we were talking over each other because neither of us was listening. I realized that I would often be waiting in between sentences for her to stop speaking so that I could speak. Not because I wanted to hear the next thing she had to say, or because her stories could actually hold my attention, but purely to ensure that I had a turn. I was simply marking time until it was my turn to speak and I realized she was doing exactly the same thing. One evening, as the both of us were walking through a park filled with autumn leaves. We got into the car and headed home. Usually we would spend the car journey chatting non-stop. The drive was usually characterized by a chaotic, cacophony of opinions and viewpoints where both parties were interrupting one another. But on that particular day the car was eerily silent. I was sitting shotgun, gazing out the car window, as she drove. And then it finally hit me. There was nothing left to say. I remember staring out the window and not seeing the leaves or the park, or even the road; I was simply staring through them and into some vast, empty expanse. I had arrived at an emotional dead end. The train wasn’t coming. And I was, well, I was done.

What makes you cringe internally? I cringe when people call themselves ‘foodies.’ I cringe harder when foodies say they ‘love’ to eat. I love to breathe, I love to sleep, I love to experience the feeling of gravity in my body but 'loving' to eat? It’s an activity you have to do in order to survive yet you act as if you are some sort of Epicurean who has transcended human banality by making me aware of your love of mastication. Yes, I understand that people like to ingest palatable items but you don’t have to ‘love’ it to make it important. It’s the same with people who love to ‘travel.’ I get it. You’ve been to a specific spot on the map. Big deal. The planet is 70% water and you have only experienced the dry land bits. How profound. You've been to Italy? Wonderful. You get back home and I'm supposed to be suitably impressed. Listen. I went to a McDonald’s in Italy. When I got back everyone was just, ‘Oh you went to a McDonald’s? That’s amazing. What was the food like?’ I just said, ‘It tastes exactly of McDonald's’ and the conversation ground to a halt. No. The people who make me cringe the most are the ones who are so un-self-aware of their own mediocrity that they think all of their activities from eating to travelling have value to others just by them performing it. That's another thing. In fact let me include this separate note. The second thing that makes me almost literally cringe is when people write ‘I’m not *insert some sort of virtue* *insert a word in a sentence implying someone’s value* but…’ and then they’re about to say or write something completely at odds with the virtue they have just mentioned. They’re not necessarily being dishonest the overwhelming majority of the time. They simply can’t see the wood for the trees.

What was a red flag that made you stop talking to a person immediately? When someone immediately reveals themselves to be a person who talks badly, in any form, about other people i.e. gossip or talk behind others’ backs, my brain automatically switches off all circuits related to continuing a conversation. I have known people who were very discreet, thoughtful and agreeable in person but the moment they get back to their workplace, their home environment, their social circle etc they turn into a raging torrent of negativity and criticism about the same people they were just laughing and joking with. The word 'hypocrite' gets thrown around a lot when people are trying to describe others. We all have certain characteristics to get along with other people, especially if we have to see them every day, however the people I’m talking about here would display a constant barrage of negativity and criticism and will eventually be backstabbing the same people they profess to admire the next time around. I have no time for such people. I understand that people have to vent, that people are entitled to share their frustrations, however there is a difference between venting and creating a habit that has become a ritual. If you are constantly being negative and critical about the world around you and always looking for negativity then I don’t need to know about it. My intention is to be happy. Most people are, to a certain extent, self centred and concerned with their own well-being and are less concerned about the feelings of those around them so it’s always best to be courteous and not project your shit on to others. I don't want to know. I have no time to deal with that. One of the reasons why I became an usher was to ensure that I was dealing with only paying customers.

What is the strangest thing a truck driver has seen while driving? I don't know that it’s the strangest thing I’ve seen because after 30 years of driving, strange is pretty much par for the course, but I do remember one instance that sticks in my mind from my very early years on the road. I was driving late at night, or more accurately, early in the morning on the interstate near some rural area in the Midwest, where I often got contracts. I rounded a bend, and in the distance, maybe half a mile ahead, I saw a bright, pulsating light hovering in the sky, not moving. It was like a giant, ethereal disco ball hanging there over the fields. I slowed down, figuring it was some kind of construction equipment or maybe a helicopter doing some aerial survey work; though neither seemed to fit, especially at four in the morning. As I got closer, the light began to change colors, flashing from blue to green to red, like some kind of cosmic Christmas display. My CB radio was dead silent. No other truckers around. Just me, the open road, and this otherworldly light show. I'm not one to scare easily, but my hair started to tingle. As I got closer, as the light grew larger, it wasn't any sort of aircraft or construction device. It was a perfect, shimmering sphere, hovering just a few feet above the ground. It emitted a soft, humming sound; no visible means of support. Then, as suddenly as it had appeared, it blinked out, gone. Vanished. Just like that. I pulled over, walked around, and checked for any trace of anything, but there wasn't a single one. Not a mark on the grass. Nothing. I figured it was just a trick of the light or perhaps my tired mind playing tricks on me. But I’ve never forgotten that night, how I felt something alien, something else.

Did you ever stop caring about how old you are? I stopped caring about how old I was a long time ago. Maybe it was the day I realised that the constant, unyielding march of time wasn't something I could control. Or maybe, more likely, it was when I worked out that nobody else really gave a damn either. Seriously, try as I might, I could never conjure up a sense of wonder about my birthday. There was no grand revelation for me, no sudden epiphany. I suspect I was born old. The only time I ever became remotely aware of my age was when some officious individual at the DMV made a big deal out of my driver's license. Other than that I only realise it when looking at old pictures. Maybe I would have felt differently when I was born in a different century. I'm speaking in jest of course. Even in the 1990s, when I felt like I was truly living, I barely registered the passage of years. Time was just a blurry, indistinct backdrop to the endless unfolding of events, like the credits scrolling by at the end of a movie. I could never truly embrace my youth. A shame really. I wasn't one for 'living in the moment' either. I’d always be the one thinking about the ‘what ifs;’ the ‘what if I’d done this?’ or ‘what if I’d done that?’ One of the hallmarks of my personality. So the inevitable passage of time, the accumulation of years, was just another element of the relentless, unstoppable flow, like a river meandering towards the sea.
