And I was content to float along with it, or at least in part. Nowadays I don't give a damn.

What is your scariest driving on a dark and lonely road at night story? It was late, or perhaps early, depending on how you looked at it. Four in the morning. I was driving back to the city after a weekend visit with family out in the country. The road was a long stretch, a ribbon unfurling under the oppressive darkness. No streetlights, just the occasional flicker from a farmhouse miles away. The radio was dead silent, the only sound the hum of the engine and the rhythmic swish of the windshield wipers, battling the persistent drizzle. I’ve always had a vivid imagination, something my sisters and I would utilise to scare each other senseless as children. Every shadow seemed to have a presence, every sound to distort itself into something sinister. About an hour into the drive, my headlights caught a figure standing on the side of the road. Tall, gaunt, and still as a statue. I slammed on the brakes, heart leaping into my throat. The figure didn't move. Just...stood there. Frozen in the beam of my headlights. I squinted, tried to make out details. It was wearing a long coat, its face obscured by the shadow of a wide-brimmed hat. I could feel the blood drain from my face. The thought that, perhaps, it wasn’t a human flooded through me. Perhaps it was an apparition, or some creature from the darkest, remotest fantasies. My survival instincts kicked in. Adrenaline surging, I put the car in reverse and floored it. It wouldn't be the first time I drove away from something that might or might not be there. I drove for what seemed like an eternity, peering into the rearview mirror. Nothing. Just the empty, wet road. I slowed down eventually. The lingering fear gradually began to subside, replaced by a nagging unease. In my state of panic, I'm sure I imagined most or all of it. A trick of the light, a scarecrow, a billboard that looked like a person. I resumed my route and soon, the sun slowly, timidly began to rise, the world slowly shedding its darkness and revealing its secrets, or lack thereof.

What are the best episodes of the original Twilight Zone TV series? I'm partial to the episodes that really leaned into the uncanny, the unsettling, the ones that burrowed under your skin and stayed there long after the credits rolled. "The Eye of the Beholder," with its unforgettable twist revealing the "monstrous" form of the beautiful protagonist, always lingers in my mind. It's a masterclass in visual storytelling and societal commentary, a stark reminder of how our perceptions can be warped and how easily we can be controlled by the opinions of others. Then there's "To Serve Man," a tale that masterfully mixes suspense with dread. Just the title alone evokes a chilling ambiguity, and the reveal, when it comes, is both shocking and darkly humorous. It's a perfect example of the show's ability to weave together science fiction, social satire, and a healthy dose of existential fear. "Nightmare at 20,000 Feet" is another standout, the kind of episode that transforms the mundane act of flying into a claustrophobic descent into madness. William Shatner's performance is iconic, and the creature on the wing is genuinely terrifying, a testament to the power of suggestion and the ability to create tension with limited resources. The episode's simple premise, the slow build of paranoia, and the inevitable climax make it a truly unforgettable entry. And of course, "The Monsters Are Due on Maple Street" deserves its place in any discussion of the best of the series. It's a powerful allegory about fear, prejudice, and the dangers of mob mentality, a cautionary tale that feels as relevant today as it did when it first aired.

Was Shelley Duvall considered attractive? Shelley Duvall's physical appearance was certainly… unique. In the early days of her career, she had a certain gamine charm, but it wasn't the conventional Hollywood beauty that dominated the screens. She possessed a quirky, almost ethereal quality that directors found captivating. Her eyes, wide and expressive, often conveyed a sense of vulnerability, adding to the oddball allure. In later years, the toll of the industry and, perhaps, of life itself, etched lines and shadows onto her face, altering her features. Whether one considered her ‘attractive' is subjective, a matter of individual taste. Her persona, too, was unconventional. She projected an offbeat vulnerability that was almost childlike. She exuded a sense of otherness, a quality many found fascinating, others, perhaps, unsettling. She was never a bombshell, a pin-up, or your typical screen siren. She was, however, unforgettable. Her appeal was in her individuality, her ability to inhabit characters that existed on the fringes of reality. She was often perceived as strange, which perhaps only added to her charm. Her presence was like a wildflower growing in a crack in the pavement: resilient and unusual. Shelley Duvall was not conventionally attractive, but she was undeniably memorable. In retrospect, one could argue that her unconventional beauty was, in its own way, far more striking than any perfectly sculpted Hollywood facade.

What one thing did your father do that left your mother sobbing? My father, a man of few words, was not accustomed to grand displays of emotion. Consequently, I have a multitude of memories of him as the strong silent type. As children it meant that he was a provider, a protector, the undisputed leader of the clan. As a child, he was a heroic figure. As an adult, the opposite was the case. Still, I’m at a loss to recall his interactions with my mother, a woman who had zero problem expressing her emotions in the most theatrical, loud fashion. This is not to say that all things were harmonious in our household. There were numerous quarrels. I would be put to bed early to not hear the drama of their arguments. Sometimes in the morning I’d find my mother red eyed. What I cannot recall when I was a child was a long time. It wasn't until my late teens when my memory started to form a complete picture. My father wasn't a ‘bad’ man, nor was he a villain. He was just so thoroughly emotionally detached. He was there, the family breadwinner, but remained largely a ghost in the house. He never volunteered a story about himself or his past. His hobbies were the same as that of the stereotyped working class bloke: watching sports on the TV and tinkering with his car. My mother worked harder and more efficiently. The only thing I remember him talking about besides those topics was the state of the economy or how the politicians were so crooked. It was rare for him to participate in gatherings or spend any amount of time with friends or relatives. But in short, in a household dominated by two very large personalities, he was very much a quiet observer. Years later I was going through my parent’s old photo albums. I came upon one of those photos, which were taken from the late 60s/early 70s. The photo was of my father and mother grinning at the camera. They were at a wedding. My parents were very young. They were both beautiful and looked incredibly happy. My father's arm was wrapped snug around my mother's waist. On the back of the photo were the words, written in my mother's handwriting: ‘That's the year he told me he had cancer and lied about it, and my world broke.’ I was shocked. I knew that my father was sick, but I had no idea he had cancer. More importantly, I had no idea my father was so deceitful. It was shocking, and it was the only time I could readily recall that my father did something that made my mother cry.

What screams "I'm low class"? Perhaps this answer is too subjective and is a matter of personal opinion. But I'll give it a shot. A few things can scream ‘I’m low class.’ It’s a subtle game, not an obvious one. One may have money; one may not. But some actions or personal traits will almost always give someone away. The use of mobile phone in a loud or inappropriate manner is one. Playing music or videos loudly on a phone in public transport, restaurants, or anywhere for that matter is a big indicator. The ‘me’ generation have always done this. It is the classic definition of ‘low class.’ One must consider those around you. Another one. Bad grammar, bad spelling and poor sentence construction, especially online or in print. I am not saying that everyone must be a grammar expert or a poet, but it's obvious to see someone with an extremely poor grasp of the English language. Another one is being rude to service staff. Whether it's a waiter, store clerk, or any service person, treating them with disrespect is a sign of low class. It speaks volumes about a person's character and their upbringing.

What guitarists do you think have the most emotionally moving solos? For me, the pantheon of guitarists who can truly make the instrument *weep* comprises a select few. It’s not always about technical prowess, the speed of their fingers across the fretboard, or how many notes they can cram into a single bar. It’s about the raw emotion, the ability to translate feelings directly from the soul to the speaker and into a tangible melody. Jimi Hendrix, of course, reigns supreme. His solos were less about notes and more about sonic landscapes, a vibrant mix of pain, euphoria, and sheer, untamed energy. His Woodstock rendition of the Star-Spangled Banner is the epitome of guitar as an emotional vessel. Then there’s David Gilmour. Where Hendrix was a tornado of sound, Gilmour was a gentle, mournful breeze. His solos with Pink Floyd, particular on the songs "Comfortably Numb" and "Time", are almost unbearably beautiful, each note carefully placed and dripping with melancholy, creating a sublime, transcendent experience every single time. And of course, there's Slash. While he might be known for his iconic riffs, his solos, such as the one in "November Rain" are heartbreakingly vulnerable; it's a raw, almost primal scream of heartbreak and loss. Speaking of primal screams, I would add Jimmy Page. His work with Led Zeppelin, from the heavy blues of "Since I've Been Loving You" to the epic grandeur of "Stairway to Heaven,” showcased an incredible range of expression. He could conjure both delicate beauty and raw power, often within a single solo. Finally, I'd add Jeff Beck, a true master of the instrument. His solos often defy categorization, but they consistently communicate deep emotion. His use of the tremolo arm, the way he bends notes, creates a sound that is all his own, a sonic equivalent of a laugh, sob, or tender touch.

Have you ever been seen naked by somebody or saw somebody naked accidentally? A few times, yes. I recall a particularly mortifying incident during my college years. I was sharing a cramped apartment with a couple of friends—a real shoebox of a place. One sweltering summer afternoon, I decided to take a quick shower to cool off. The bathroom, as always, was a humid, claustrophobic space, and the shower curtain was a flimsy, translucent affair. As I was lathering up, I heard the distinct sound of my roommate's key in the lock. Before I had a chance to react, the door swung open, and there he stood, a look of utter surprise plastered across his face. He stammered an apology and quickly retreated, but the image—both of him seeing me and the mortification on his face—is still etched in my memory. Another time, I was at a public swimming pool, minding my own business, when a young woman lost her bikini top after diving into the pool. It was an unavoidable accident, and everyone averted their gaze out of respect. Nonetheless, it was pretty awkward.

What actor or actress got cast in a role that they normally wouldn't play and absolutely crushed it? The first actor that comes to mind is Heath Ledger in The Dark Knight. Never in a million years would you have expected the pretty-boy heartthrob from a string of romantic comedies and period dramas to deliver a portrayal of the Joker that would not only redefine the character but also etch itself into cinematic history. Ledger, prior to that performance, was primarily known for roles that showcased his boyish charm and good looks. His casting as the Joker was met with a fair amount of skepticism, even derision from some quarters, but Ledger silenced all naysayers with a performance that was nothing short of breathtaking. Watching him on screen, you weren't seeing Heath Ledger, the actor, you were seeing the Joker, a force of pure, unadulterated chaos. His commitment to the role, his willingness to delve into the character's darkness, and his meticulous attention to detail were evident in every twitch, every cackle, and every deranged utterance. It's a testament to Ledger's talent that he completely transformed himself, shedding his previous persona and immersing himself so fully in the role that it's impossible to imagine anyone else playing the Joker with such chilling brilliance. The fact that he won a posthumous Academy Award for his performance speaks volumes about its impact. It's a shining example of an actor pushing the boundaries of their craft, taking a risk, and succeeding beyond all expectations. Another prime example would be Bryan Cranston in Breaking Bad. Before portraying Walter White, Cranston was best known for his comedic roles, most notably as the lovable, hapless father in Malcolm in the Middle. Could the affable, somewhat goofy Cranston truly embody a chemistry teacher turned meth kingpin? The answer, as it turned out, was a resounding yes. Cranston brought a depth and complexity to Walter White that was nothing short of phenomenal. He began as a sympathetic character, a man driven to desperate measures by circumstance, and gradually, chillingly, transformed into a ruthless, power-hungry villain. Cranston's performance was a masterclass in character development. He flawlessly conveyed White’s intelligence, vulnerability, simmering rage, and gradual descent into moral depravity. It was a transformative role that not only showcased Cranston's incredible range but permanently redefined his career. He proved that an actor could defy typecasting and achieve the unthinkable by taking us on an unforgettable journey into the dark heart and mind of a man consumed by ego.

What Scorsese film would have been better if directed by Spielberg and vice versa? This is not an easy question to answer. Both directors are titans of cinema, and their distinct styles are immediately recognizable. Scorsese, the master of the urban grit, the volatile underworld, the raw emotion, and complex flawed characters set against the backdrop of a bustling cityscape. Then you have Spielberg. The purveyor of wonder and childhood. Wholesomeness, optimism, the all-American hero and family values amidst a backdrop of grand scope, operatic score and a master of the tracking shot. The two directors are opposites so in a sense you’re asking me what is better? Chalk or cheese? In my opinion the best Scorsese movie is Goodfellas, an American crime film so iconic that it is difficult for me to fathom anyone but Scorsese directing it. The characters, plot and violence requires the distinct gritty eye of Scorsese. The same can be said for The Departed. Spielberg would have directed an okay movie but it would have been too polished and lost the edge that Scorsese brought to them. For Spielberg, I would say the best movie he made is E.T. the Extra-Terrestrial, a family movie that is a true visual spectacle. Spielberg is a master of the camera and is second to none when it comes to pure movie wizardry. The two directors are excellent at what they do. With all the respect and reverence that I possess for them.  The continuation: A Scorsese-directed E.T. would be a very different film, very un-Spielbergian. I would not have the optimism, magic and pure sense of wonderment of the original. The film would likely be more downbeat, perhaps exploring the loneliness of Elliott and his difficult home life. It would dwell on the street life and gang culture of suburban L.A. The use of cinematography may feature more close-ups of the children, their vulnerability, and their inner lives. This would be juxtaposed with the mundane reality of everyday life. A more somber soundtrack would accompany the film. A contrast from that of John Williams’ score with hints of heavy guitars, a more gritty, realistic tone. A Scorsese version of E.T. might feature a more complex and ambiguous portrayal of the adults in Elliott's life. A more realistic view of divorce and dysfunctional family life, so that the escapism E.T. represents would be all the more crucial. The film would lose the sense of innocence, and the pure joy of Spielberg's version, but would be likely be a more moving and thought-provoking film. In the end it would not have been better, just different.

How did your boss respond when you told him/her you quit? My experiences quitting jobs have always been varied, depending on management style and the specifics of my departure. I’ve had bosses who took it with apparent stoicism, offering a polite farewell and quickly moving on, seemingly unfazed. Others reacted with thinly veiled disappointment, attempting to cajole me into reconsidering, dangling the false pretences of promotions and salary raises, while I stared blankly at them as if I'd just been informed I could speak Mandarin. Then there were those who displayed genuine surprise, coupled with a reluctant acceptance, saying something along the lines of: ‘Well, I suppose you know what's best.’ Perhaps the most memorable reaction, however, was a blend of all three, a man known for his mercurial temperament. His response to my resignation was initially one of detached indifference, a casual ‘Oh, right,’ followed by a barely perceptible flicker of something akin to hurt. This was immediately succeeded by a clumsy attempt to dissuade me, claiming that I was an invaluable asset to the team, before finally lapsing into a resigned sigh and a muttered, ‘Well, good luck.’ I found that particularly amusing.

Have you ever lost any respect for someone instantly? It's a common phenomenon, isn't it? That sudden shift in perception, the moment the pedestal crumbles, and the person you once admired plummets from grace. A single action, a careless word, a glimpse behind the curtain, and *poof* – the illusion shatters. I have, countless times, and it's rarely a pleasant experience. Sometimes it's petty, driven by a fleeting moment of moral superiority, a judgmental twitch as someone fails to live up to my own absurdly high standards. Other times, it’s a slow burn, a gradual erosion of respect brought about by consistent behavior that grates on my sensibilities. There are folks, for example, that I find quite easy to summarily dismiss from my good books for seemingly nothing. You know the type – the ones who dominate every conversation, talking over others, rarely listening, constantly needing to be the center of attention. Or the ones who proudly and loudly proclaim their supposedly virtuous opinions while simultaneously proving to be the most bigoted, intolerant individuals one can come across. The hypocrisy is just too rich to stomach. And then there are the moments, the ones that sting, when a person’s true character is revealed, a deep-seated flaw laid bare. The moment, for instance, when a person shows themselves to be cruel or spiteful or selfish when you know they're capable of far more than they are showing. That's the kind of loss of respect that leaves a sour taste lingering long after the moment has passed. It's a brutal realization that leaves you thinking, ‘Well, fuck, I thought you were better than that, and I was clearly wrong.’

What are some examples of style without substance in writers? Many of the most popular self-help books and amateur fiction pieces you come across these days boast a distinct lack of substance yet try to compensate by throwing fancy words left, right, and center and using the most convoluted sentence structures. Authors of this variety believe that if they just write something long enough and sprinkle in all the correct buzzwords, erudite vocabulary and use every trope in the book, regardless of whether it actually fits the narrative, then they must, by default, be good writers. It's the literary equivalent of putting a cheap suit on a scruffy looking homeless guy and expecting him to suddenly look like a Bond villain. This style is often used to hide a lack of actual ideas and to deceive the audience with the illusion of profundity. The stories may lack any compelling characters, the plots may be predictable, and the themes explored may be shallow and uninspired. But the writer hopes that the reader will be so busy trying to decipher the meaning of each individual sentence, with its obscure references and long-winded phrasing, that they won't notice the emptiness at the core of the work. I once read an amateur novel where the author constantly used words with a minimum of 4 syllables just to make sure the reader knew how ‘clever’ he was. He also used very long paragraphs but he didn't write anything concrete or interesting. The story was about a detective who was very sad over his divorced wife. The author used the word ‘melancholy’ in every other sentence. If I took a shot for every time that word pops up I’d probably be dead. The best writers have so much substance that they don't need to add so much style. The style is just a consequence of the writer’s thought process.

What is something that Hollywood always gets wrong? Hollywood loves to portray intellectuals and academics as either eccentric buffoons, detached from reality, or as power-hungry Machiavellians, scheming in secret, or sometimes, a combination of both. It’s a trope as old as the medium. My perspective comes from a lifetime of being surrounded by these people. I grew up in a university town, my parents, siblings and my first and most consistent circle of friends were professors, teachers, librarians. My extended family were artists, writers, journalists, even politicians. I can say from experience that most of them are just ordinary folk trying to get through the day. They might have a particular set of interests or a specific expertise, but they’re not all sitting around plotting world domination or forgetting the simple things in life like how to tie their shoelaces. The thing about any profession, be it professional, blue collar, creative whatever it is, that you're drawn to, is the variety. You get all kinds of people, not just one neatly packaged stereotype that can be easily parodied for entertainment purposes. I’ve known brilliant academics who couldn’t boil an egg, just as I’ve known some who are handy in the kitchen and at home DIY. I’ve known people who enjoy nothing more than a lively debate and others who would rather retreat to the quiet of a library or a solitary walk in the park. Hollywood seems to miss this fundamental point, favouring broad strokes and clichés over something that represents the depth of human experience. Edit: To the people in the comments, who are arguing that the characters that Hollywood portrays are merely reflecting a certain element in society, I completely agree. However, the problem is in the way those elements are often portrayed, presented without dimension, nuance or proper context. Hollywood has to be more honest about its representation of people.

Is it superficial that I lost interest in a guy because he proudly said that he hasn't read any book in his life? Maybe. I get it. It’s a red flag, isn’t it? It’s a sign, to you, maybe, that this person lacks curiosity, doesn’t value knowledge, and is probably dull as dishwater. And it’s very easy to get turned off by a lack of intellectual pursuits and a certain ignorance to the world’s vastness. But is it superficial to dismiss this guy? Are you being a snob? I don’t know. There are lots of ways to look at it. Some of the greatest people in history haven’t been bookworms. Some of the worst people in history have been huge readers. Reading a book isn’t exactly a sign of saintliness. It doesn’t automatically make someone interesting or intelligent. Plenty of people read, and read, and read, and still come across as boring and vapid. Lots of people have no problem reading, but still fail to grasp the concepts of the world around them.

What is your most interesting encounter with the police? When I was about 14 or 15, I was skateboarding with a couple of friends at night in a public park. We weren't doing anything wrong, just enjoying the cool night air and the thrill of the ride. The park was mostly empty, and the only light came from the distant street lamps, which cast long, dancing shadows across the asphalt. Suddenly, we heard the unmistakable sound of a police siren drawing closer. Our hearts started to pound in our chests. We knew we weren't breaking any laws, but there’s still a certain innate fear of law enforcement for any teenager. The patrol car screeched to a halt in front of us, its headlights blinding. A stern-faced officer, a relatively beefy gentleman, emerged, his hand resting on the sidearm at his hip. Another officer, a considerably younger woman with a more affable expression, followed. The male officer approached us and demanded to know what we were doing. We explained that we were just skating, and that we hadn’t done anything wrong. He eyeballed us suspiciously, peering at our boards and the faded logos and cracked wheels. "You know it's late, right? There's a curfew for minors," he growled. I think the curfew in question started at 10 pm. I think it was about 10.30 pm. We mumbled apologies, our voices filled with the kind of nervousness only teenagers experiencing their first encounter with the law can truly understand. The male officer continued to lecture us for a good five minutes about responsibility and all that righteous jazz. The female officer, on the other hand, seemed more understanding, I don’t think she enjoyed her job. She gently suggested we head home. She had a kind voice. As the male officer finished his speech, he gestured for us to leave. We were relieved, but also confused, because we genuinely didn't think we had done anything wrong. As we were packing up, the female officer took a step towards us ‘Just so you know,’ she said, her voice barely above a whisper, ‘He's like this. This is his first week.’ She turned to the male officer and then walked back to the car and let us go on our way. That encounter stuck with me, not because we got in trouble, or were even slightly roughed up, but because of that one small act of rebellion from the other officer. It told a story of a system that had its issues. A story that everyone knows.

Why would I kill a mugger in self-defense? Are my valuables worth more than their life? This touches on a fascinating moral quandary, doesn’t it? One that often boils down to a deeply entrenched understanding of value. Would I take another human being's life to protect a wallet, a phone, or even a family heirloom? I suppose the answer is contingent, isn’t it? Does the mugger possess a weapon? Are they threatening me or others? Am I in a position to retreat and avoid the confrontation entirely? I envision myself as pacifistic. I’d like to think that survival is instinctual, so if my physical safety is at risk, the calculus shifts. But even then, the weight of taking a life, the psychological and spiritual ramifications, would be enormous. Conversely, if my life were not on the line, then yes, I'd let the mugger take whatever he pleases. One should never escalate unnecessary violence. The loss of property, while distressing, is ultimately replaceable. The loss of a life, however, is not. It’s a permanent state. It’s also a consequence of the choices one makes. To me, violence, is a terrible choice. But, in the end, my decision is the one that has to be made. Some might say that such considerations are naive. The tough love type would say that I need to be more realistic and take a life. Life has no rules, no guidelines, no guarantees. And yet, despite all of this, I find myself leaning towards valuing life over things.
What are the most annoying things customers do at your restaurant/store? The most annoying thing

What "poverty food" is actually really delicious? Being a son of Trinidadian parents I grew up with a fairly unique pallet for poor people's food. We didn't really have a lot of money when I was a kid, so the meals we ate were always a bit *different* from what my friends would have. I loved them. My friends not so much. A lot of what we had was canned, salted, or pickled foods from the local supermarkets. A lot of the food was imported goods like canned corned beef, canned sardines, and the like. Being a Caribbean island, we would also have local staples such as callaloo soup, split peas, or bake and saltfish as we called it. I will always have an affinity and love for these simple meals, and I will always have an almost instinctive repulsion towards anything remotely resembling middle-class haute cuisine. My friends and relatives would always be bemused by my choices. 'Why," they would ask, "would you choose to eat this?'. This would often happen when visiting extended family or friends. Their kitchens always seemed to be filled with food that my family did not usually have. Food that in my eyes seemed to be 'too much' and I didn't know what to do with it. Food that, to me, tasted weird. I have to admit that eating food from other people's houses was a traumatic experience during my formative years. I still remember going over to my cousin's house. My cousin's mother spent an inexplicable amount of time cooking a bunch of what looked like plain spaghetti, some pre-packed chicken nuggets and a side of french fries. After my initial delight at the novelty of it all I could not bring myself to finish it. The taste was weird, and the texture felt wrong. The memory of it still makes me shudder and question my own appetite for 'middle-class' food. But I have grown and diversified and am no longer so intransigent about these things - though corned beef, sardines, and bake and saltfish, still hit the spot.

What's the best "tourist trap" you've ever fallen into? Niagara Falls, baby. Not the American side, mind you - that's a festering cesspool of overpriced hotdog stands and greasy souvenir shops. No, I'm talking about the Canadian side, all glitz and glam, flashing lights and casinos. I went there with my wife and two rugrats expecting a monumental letdown, a total waste of time and money. I'd heard all the horror stories. Tourist traps were not something I was familiar with. I'm not the kind of person who goes on tours, I like to figure it all out myself. So I was completely unprepared for the experience, I was sure it was going to be a let down. Everything I’d read, gleaned from second-hand accounts and the internet, had prepared me for disappointment. What I got, however, was pure, unadulterated escapism. The falls themselves, of course, were magnificent. Mother Nature, at her most sublime. But it was the spectacle that the city had crafted around them that really got me. It was a feast for the senses, a riot of colors, sounds, and smells. Our kids had a blast. We rode the Maid of the Mist and got soaked to the bone, we explored the tunnels behind the falls and felt the thunder of the water. We ate at gaudy themed restaurants with names like “Rainforest Cafe.” We even bought a few ridiculously overpriced souvenirs. Yes, it was all a gigantic, crass, commercial enterprise, designed to extract every last dollar from the unsuspecting tourist. And yes, I loved every single minute of it. When we hit the road I was fully aware of the fact that I had been completely ripped off, every experience had a price-tag that was far beyond what was reasonable for an average middle-class family, but the fun and the memories were priceless. It was money well spent. I'd do it all again in a heartbeat. It's the kind of trap that you want to get caught in, a guilty pleasure, a reminder that sometimes, it's okay to be a sucker.

What's the funniest thing you heard in a movie theater? Honestly, most of the funniest things I've heard in a movie theater weren't from the movie itself. It was from the audience. People at the movies. Or kids in the movies. I recall one time when I went to see a Pixar movie with a friend. This was before smartphones were ubiquitous, so people were more engaged with the film, with the kids in the theater. Some kid, probably no more than seven years old, was sitting a few rows behind us. The movie was building to a crescendo. A big, dramatic moment. Something the studio had spent several million dollars to build. Then came the kid, with a voice that was not very loud but loud enough to be noticed by everyone in the theater: "Mommy, I gotta poop!" The timing was sublime, absolutely perfect. Everyone in the theater, including the kid’s mother, started to laugh. The scene was ruined, but it didn't matter. We were all united in laughter, which is really the point of going to the movies in the first place. Another instance which was funny for similar reasons to the previous story: I was watching a superhero movie. These days there are so many of them. The hero in a tough spot, about to be defeated by the bad guy. The tension was palpable. Someone in the audience, a woman, let out a loud, exasperated sigh, clearly invested in what would happen next. Out of nowhere… “Oh, come on!” she exclaimed. Again, the comedic timing was impeccable. It sliced through the tension like a lightsaber. People erupted in laughter. The woman looked mortified, but couldn't help but smile. It's these unexpected moments, the real-life drama interjecting itself into the fictional world, that you remember long after the credits roll. Sometimes real life is far funnier more entertaining than anything Hollywood can come up with. Edit: It's amazing how many people enjoyed this answer and decided to upvote it and share their own movie theater experiences. It's great to feel a communal experience through these answers.

Have you ever come back to your vehicle only to find something quite unexpected? Last week I returned to my car after doing some shopping and found a small, beautifully wrapped gift box perched neatly on the hood. My first reaction was, naturally, abject bewilderment. What in the blue blazes was going on? I had no idea what it could be. I looked around, half-expecting a camera crew to jump out and yell "Surprise!" as if I were some sort of unwitting contestant on a hidden camera show, but the parking lot was deserted. This was not uncommon, the shopping complex where I live is in the middle of nowhere. The stores I visit offer a sparse range of goods at inflated prices, leaving only a handful of customers, mostly old, poor, and forgotten. Perhaps this was it, the setup to the local lottery's new promotional campaign. Some sort of cryptic treasure hunt. I approached the vehicle with trepidation, half-expecting a bomb and half-expecting a romantic gesture. The box wasn't heavy, so that at least was a good sign. On top of the lid was a handwritten note. I opened it. Inside it read: "We know what you did." Now that was unexpected indeed. I started to sweat, what did I do? I racked my brain to think of something I knew would get me in trouble. The car was fine but whoever left it knew that I had an old beater car that was just the wreck on the side of the road. The car was a write off, a piece of junk. I had every intention of scrapping it. Before I did. I let a homeless man sleep in it. He was grateful. I also saw it as a better use of the car. Had he also left the gift? He was old and looked like he was homeless. He was just grateful for the offer. I had to open the present, the suspense was killing me. I finally tore through the gift wrap and found, inside, a shiny new key.

What screams "I'm pretending to be upper class"? I have noticed a trend; the proliferation of words used in reference to ‘rustic simplicity,’ as though their provenance, their very being is a byproduct of a life lived among the French aristocracy or, at least, the landed gentry. The use of words like *bespoke*, *artisanal*, and *curated* are the most egregious examples. They are often deployed by people whose idea of *country living* is based on watching aspirational lifestyle movies set in Martha's Vineyard. There is the insistence on *hand-poured candles*, even in the face of obvious and cheap mass production. Then there’s the ubiquitous rise in *organic* this and *farm-to-table* that. As if our forebears, even just a couple of generations removed, didn't eat organically or have their food go from the farm to the table. All of this points to a deep-seated insecurity, an attempt to elevate themselves to a social class they do not belong to. They are, in fact, doing the exact opposite. The pretension is transparent. The attempt clumsy. The very act reveals them to be exactly what they don’t want to be. And that makes it an even more laughable display. The other big signal is the pretentious accent. I have noticed people who otherwise speak with a perfectly competent regional accent suddenly adopt a faux-British or a faux-French. Often they are not even consistent with the accent. One minute it's a cut glass Queen's English, and the next it's a garbled approximation of a Parisian boulangerie worker. A dead giveaway is when one is forced to hear an entirely inappropriate, contrived accent when talking to a customer service representative at a call centre. The whole charade is, of course, pathetic. And it's usually all for show, the social media post to flaunt their lives and make others feel inadequate. The real upper class doesn't need to flaunt. They simply *are*. They don't need to pretend; and usually they’re not at all interested in such a thing.

What movies can you watch all the time and never get tired of watching? There are two films that I can watch over and over again, and still find fresh laughs with each viewing, these are “So I Married an Axe Murderer” and “Galaxy Quest.” “So I Married an Axe Murderer” is crammed full of little details and humor that one can only notice after repeated viewings. The performances of the main cast in that movie are a joy to watch. Just the bit where Charlie McKenzie (Mike Meyers) introduces his girlfriend Harriet (Nancy Travis) to his parents is comedy gold. But that's something that a lot of people notice. As mentioned earlier I love how obscure the movie gets. In the barbershop scene during the song "Goodnight Irene" when Harriet’s Scottish accent, is in full force, it's just so understated and low-key. What I find even more interesting is Harriet's mysterious dark past. It's an easy and effective device for the plot: The fact that someone could be hiding a dark past from an unsuspecting party is always engaging. Then there’s the cinematography and camerawork. The director cleverly uses close-up shots of Harriet and Charlie when they are doing a scene of intense, personal connection. Also that ‘camera angle’ shot where its focus is on the Axe Murderer’s hands as she holds a sharp weapon, always heightens the suspense. “Galaxy Quest” is a film that I watch over and over again because of the amazing casting and performances. The cast has done stellar work and has great chemistry together. I love Alan Rickman’s performance, as the disgruntled actor whose portrayal of the alien character Dr. Lazarus is nothing short of epic. And it helps that the entire plot, as a parody of Star Trek, is so brilliantly written and the writing never fails to come across funny.

I got an invitation to a high school reunion where I was bullied. I am successful in my career. I want the satisfaction that I’m doing better than my bullies, but I don’t want to demean myself on that level. Should I go? This is a classic dilemma, isn’t it? The allure of a reunion, the chance to flaunt your success, and maybe, just maybe, wipe the smug grins off the faces of those who made your teenage years a living hell. The desire for vindication, the sweet taste of proving them wrong – it’s a powerful motivator, a siren song for the ego. But the question is, at what cost? Are you prepared to re-enter that toxic environment, to breathe in the stale air of adolescent judgments and petty rivalries, even if for a few hours? It’s a gamble, a dance with your past self, and the outcome is never guaranteed. You could emerge victorious, basking in the envious glances of your former tormentors. Or you could find yourself once again trapped in the shadows of those painful memories, the wounds of those bygone days, re-opened and festering. Is it worth the risk of reliving those experiences, of allowing them to steal a small piece of your present joy? Think about it this way: Would your success be diminished if you didn’t go? Does the validation of those people truly matter? The answer, I suspect, lies within you. It's your choice to embrace the event or simply to let it fade away like a bad dream.

Why would homeless people rather beg on the street than get a job at McDonald’s? Let me tell you a little secret: it's not always a matter of choice. I've had a front-row seat to this particular drama. I've worked with homeless people; at a shelter, when I was still wet behind the ears. They were a mixed bag, as you'd expect from any cross-section of society. Some, yes, were frankly lazy, addicted to the dole, and content to live off the generosity of others. These chaps had a multitude of issues, from substance abuse to mental health problems, that served as a convenient shield to their inactivity. They understood the system and how to milk it. They were the outliers, the ones who gave the rest of them a bad name. Then there were the others, the quiet ones, the ones who would rather die than ask for help. These are the ones who wouldn’t take your charity. The ones who actually did things right if you gave them a leg-up. They were the ones you never saw, because they faded into the background. They were proud, stubbornly independent, and often, deeply ashamed of their situation. Many had lost everything, their homes, jobs, families, to forces beyond their control, to bad luck. The ones who, yes, would work at McDonald's given the opportunity. But many can’t. Life isn’t fair, and if it were, it wouldn't be life. They’re hampered by a lack of basic skills, a criminal record, or simply the crushing weight of despair. A gap on your resume would be a minor problem for most. For them it’s a dealbreaker. They are the ones who spend every waking moment on the street, at the mercy of the weather, hunger, disease, and the ever-present threat of violence. Many of them, I discovered, had mental health issues, which made the simple act of holding down a job impossible. They desperately needed help but were unwilling or unable to seek it. The stigma of welfare, the shame of asking for assistance, was too much to bear. And in my case, I should know.

Have you ever sabotaged food because someone was stealing it? I haven’t. My siblings and I, being the well-behaved angels we were (ahem), never stooped to such levels of petty thievery. But I’ve heard stories. Oh, the stories one hears when one has a brother. He once told me that, in his youth, he was a master of the culinary sabotage. It involved a lot of laxatives, a whole lot of chili powder, and, on one particularly memorable occasion, a generous helping of hot sauce in a batch of his own ‘secret’ chili. The intended victim? A friend who had the audacity to sneak into the kitchen and help himself to a serving. My brother, ever the meticulous planner, waited patiently for the inevitable retribution. He watched, with the gleeful anticipation of a Bond villain, as the friend, utterly unsuspecting, consumed his stolen prize. The reaction, according to my brother, was immediate and spectacular. The friend, who was a notoriously stubborn character, turned a shade of crimson usually reserved for fire trucks and proceeded to sprint directly to the nearest lavatory. My brother, meanwhile, had to bite his tongue, so the whole neighborhood did not hear his riotous laughter. From what he told me, the friend never stole his food again. Fair play I'd reckon.

Who is an actor who you think looks better older than they did when they were younger? Harrison Ford, hands down. The man was always handsome, mind you. Back in his Han Solo days, he was the effortlessly cocky, charismatic rogue with a winning smile. But somewhere along the way, as the years started to etch lines around his eyes and his hair acquired that distinguished silver streak, he evolved into something even more compelling. Perhaps it's the gravitas that comes with age, the knowing look that suggests a lifetime of experiences etched onto his face. He's become the weathered hero, the grizzled adventurer, the embodiment of quiet strength. Think of him in *Blade Runner 2049*, or even more recently, *Indiana Jones and the Dial of Destiny*. He carries a weight, a depth. There's a certain vulnerability in his aging that makes him infinitely more relatable, more human. It's a testament to his acting ability that he can convey so much with just a glance, a subtle shift in his expression. Some actors cling desperately to their youth, fighting the inevitable with every botox injection and cosmetic procedure. Ford, on the other hand, has embraced the change, allowing it to amplify his talent and charisma. He's proof that true beauty isn't about youthful perfection, but about the story written on your face – the story of a life lived, battles fought and lessons learned.

My girlfriend is mad at me for "not standing up for her.” She accidentally spilled her drink on a girl in the club. The other girl threw her drink on my girlfriend and her boyfriend shoved me. I grabbed my girlfriend and we left. What should I do? You did the right thing. What else could you have possibly done? You grabbed your girl, and you left. That's literally all you're supposed to do in that scenario. You weren't obligated to start a brawl for her. The other girl, and her boyfriend, started it; they escalated the situation. It's a nightclub, at night. These places attract intoxicated people. Intoxicated people in a crowded place with loud music and dim lighting can be unpredictable and belligerent. You'd be a fool to think that a fight wouldn't potentially end badly for you. It happens. It's not worth it. My advice? Tell your girlfriend that you did the right thing and that you weren't going to stoop to their level by getting into a physical altercation. She needs to understand that you prioritized her safety and well-being over some silly pride. It is a sign of a strong person to walk away from conflict and not get dragged into other people’s mess or drama. If she's still angry, then frankly, she has some growing up to do. Relationships don't need these unnecessary arguments.

What advice changed your life financially? It's hard to pinpoint one single instance, but rather a culmination of advice and personal observations that reshaped my financial trajectory. Growing up, my family wasn't exactly swimming in cash. We knew what it was like to stretch a dollar, make do with less, and, occasionally, scramble just to keep the lights on. So perhaps that served as a good springboard towards the importance of fiscal responsibility. My first foray into the working world, as a teenager, was at a local fast-food joint. Minimum wage, long hours, the smell of fries – you know the drill. During my downtime I read a book by Robert Kiyosaki. At the time he was a controversial financial guru as he made the then unusual recommendation of having his own employees work for him. "You've got to work for money," my boss told me with a smirk, "but Kiyosaki wants you to have your money work for you." It sounded ludicrous to someone who could barely pay off the occasional overdue library book. The boss’s words were to be etched in granite. The irony, however, was not wasted on me as my boss was a textbook example of making money. His business was a franchise and he made more money than he could spend. I ended up hating my time there and quitting after a month. The work was monotonous and the pay was abysmal. Though I hated the work, I was glad with all the practical experience I got from it. He, as an employer, was getting a much better deal. His words gave me that inspiration to start thinking about my long-term financial goals. It took many years before I’d fully understand the message, but something had been planted in my mind: the importance of acquiring assets that generate income, rather than just trading time for money. It was about the principle of investing. My boss spent his time managing other people’s earnings. I would spend mine to support my family. This idea became even more poignant when I started reading books on investing. I would never be in the same position that my boss was in. It was the single most important ingredient in building long-term wealth even though at the time I was struggling with the most basics of budgeting. I also read a lot of different books on various different types of investment vehicles. I always knew that I'd have been very good with numbers, but reading all these books was the first time in which I can actually see the logic of my numbers skills. The key was: if I could spend a dollar less than I earned, and then put that dollar to work through investment, it would grow over time. The sooner I started, the greater the compounding effect, and the earlier I could retire. The advice, as I said, wasn’t a singular eureka moment. It was a slow burn, a gradual understanding of concepts I was initially skeptical of. It was having my own working experience. It was reading books that offered different types of analysis. Perhaps the most fundamental lesson was this: there’s no magic bullet. No shortcuts. Just consistent effort, a willingness to learn, and the discipline to stick to a plan. The advice changed my life by providing me with a framework and a goal. The rest was up to me.

What has an employee said that immediately caused you to fire them? I was working in a call center, a place notorious for its high turnover and low morale. One day, a new hire, we'll call him Kevin, was training to be a customer service representative. The trainer, a dour woman named Brenda, was meticulously going over the script, emphasizing the importance of empathy and active listening. Kevin, a fresh-faced kid with perhaps too much bravado, was visibly bored. He started fidgeting, rolling his eyes and making exaggerated sighs. Brenda, God bless her, tried to soldier on. She even asked Kevin to demonstrate how he would handle a hypothetical irate customer. Kevin, leaning back in his chair with a smirk, deadpanned, "I'd probably just hang up. Life's too short to deal with whiny jerks." Brenda's face turned a shade of crimson I'd never witnessed before. Then she called me over. "I'm sorry, but could you deal with this? I'm going to go have a cigarette." A few minutes later, Kevin was packing his things and escorted out the building. The reason? What he said was not the trigger. It was the unrepentant, smirking attitude with which he offered it that sealed his fate and ensured his job did not last more than mere hours. The guy acted as if he was doing me a favor by showing up. It was an act of defiance of the entire philosophy of our call center operation and a waste of everyone's time, especially Brenda's. The call center industry is not made for people like that.

What movies do you like but everybody hates, and why? I’ve never been much for the highbrow, the critically acclaimed, or the Academy Award winners. Give me a B-movie, a schlocky horror flick, or a straight-to-video action piece any day of the week. My preferences lean towards the type of films that are generally considered dreadful, laughably bad, or just plain forgettable. Some people would be mortified at even the thought of admitting my tastes, but, hell, I don’t care. I've never understood the point of liking things just because other people like them. In this regard, my favorite film is "Battlefield Earth." Now, I know, I *know*. According to all rational estimations, this film should be considered an unmitigated disaster. It's a cinematic train wreck on par with "Plan 9 From Outer Space" and "Troll 2". It's a disaster on par with the aforementioned, the acting is atrocious, the plot, nonsensical, John Travolta's performance is the stuff of ridicule and the direction is haphazard. It's often cited as one of the worst films ever made. Yet, I genuinely enjoy it. I love it. I've seen it dozens of times. I relish in its awfulness. I'm not blind to its flaws. I recognize them, I acknowledge them, and I embrace them. There's something about the sheer audacity of its failure that I find oddly compelling. There's its over-the-top theatrics, its bizarre pseudo-religious undertones, and its relentless commitment to its own outlandish vision, even as that vision implodes in front of the audience’s very eyes. It's a masterclass in how *not* to make a film, and that, in itself, is a perverse kind of accomplishment. It’s hard to describe. It’s similar to a friend who would probably be deemed a complete buffoon when described to other people but you love them unconditionally. It’s almost guaranteed that it will bring joy to my life, I can always count on it. Beyond "Battlefield Earth," I have a soft spot for a number of other films that have been panned by critics and dismissed by most audiences. Films like "The Garbage Pail Kids Movie," the aforementioned "Troll 2," and "Howard the Duck." These movies have a certain charm to them, a naive sincerity that wins me over, in spite of their glaring deficiencies. So, yes, to quote the film, I guess, in a sense, ‘we are all Battlefield Earth’ - in the face of societal expectations, we all have our little guilty pleasures, our cinematic skeletons in the closet, and our secret cinematic shames. We shouldn’t hide them away and if others judge us, well, that’s their problem, not ours.

What disturbing rumor turned out to be true at your school? We had a high school teacher—let's call him Mr. Harrison—who taught History and English. He had been at the school for a long time, so he was well-liked, respected, and seemingly, above reproach. He was a middle-aged man, always impeccably dressed, with a dry wit and an air of intellectual superiority. The rumor started subtly, whispered in the corridors, passed between the older students: That Mr. Harrison was involved with a student. At first, it was just speculation, fueled by hushed tones and knowing looks. There was the persistent observation of him lingering after school hours with a particular girl, let’s call her Sarah, who was undeniably bright and attractive, and obviously flattered by the attention of her teacher. Then things got more specific. Whispers of late-night phone calls. Stories of Sarah being seen leaving his house. These whispers, of course, were quickly dismissed by most of the students as mere gossip—the idle chatter of teenagers. I myself did not give the rumour much thought, not at first anyway. Mr. Harrison had always seemed incredibly professional, and frankly, rather intimidating. It all seemed so outlandish. But then, the whispers became louder, more brazen. It was said that Sarah's grades were improving dramatically, and the school, in true negligent form, was turning a blind eye to the matter. Then people started saying that Sarah had indeed moved into his private home. It was around this time that our school principal called an emergency assembly for a special announcement. I still don't know or recall if the announcement was to make certain that an investigation will go ahead or to quell the rumor. It didn't matter. The truth became a terrifying reality within a moment. His voice was barely audible, but his face contorted into a moment of pure anguish. He confirmed the worst. He was, indeed, having an affair with a student. All the air was sucked out of the room. Silence. Then, pandemonium. It was a day I will never forget. Mr Harrison was immediately fired, and his reputation was in tatters. Sarah, of course, was pulled out from the school and her life, along with those of us in the student body who saw her in the halls of our respective schools, would never be the same. Looking back, I can't help but feel a sense of disgust and betrayal. Not only for Mr. Harrison's actions, but also for the school's inaction and denial. It was a dark secret, exposed in the cruel light of reality. It revealed to me that the most stable, respectable beings can commit the basest of acts. More than that, the incident taught me how deeply flawed the adults in one’s lives can actually be.

Which TV shows were popular when you were younger that would flop today? Why? That's a fun question. I remember being completely obsessed with Knight Rider as a kid. The show with David Hasselhoff and KITT, the talking car. Complete 80's perfection. The music, the fashion, the special effects, the unbelievable plots. I thought the car was sentient. Now, watching the show as an adult (thank you YouTube) and being a little more aware, I can see that the show has a lot of problems that would make it a non-starter today. The acting is wooden, the plots are paper-thin and, let's be honest, the car looks ridiculously outdated. As a car enthusiast, I would have known better. The special effects, by today's standards, look terrible. Even by 80's standards they were not great. There are certain shows, like say the original Star Trek, who did all they could with the limited budgets available at the time and the production design shows this effort, but Knight Rider looks cheaply made and the entire premise is completely daft. In the 80s there was a sense of escapism. Television and movies were meant to be a form of pure entertainment. Not all the time, but more so than today. Reality wasn’t as in your face as it is now. People didn't nitpick every frame of a tv show or scrutinise every minute detail like they do today. Viewers were more willing to suspend their disbelief and go along for the ride. Today's audiences are far more discerning. They want realism, complexity, and depth, and even if they don’t they are inundated with TV shows and movies that do offer such things. Knight Rider, with its simplistic plots and cheesy dialogue, could not compete. The show tried to revive itself in the early 2000's but even that was a flop. I don’t know how a show with a cool car and the Hoff would even fail. Some things, it seems, are best left in the past.

The Good, the Bad & the Ugly is an amazing movie but I never understood the scene involving Tuco and his monk brother. As much as it was an emotional scene, it did not advance the movie plot at all. Did Leone ever explain why he added the scene? I've always been intrigued by how Sergio Leone, like a masterful painter, could use vast landscapes and prolonged moments of silence to build tension and tell a story. The scene you're referring to, with Tuco and his brother, the monk, is a prime example. While it might seem extraneous, a brief pause in the unrelenting pursuit of gold, it offers a glimpse into Tuco's soul. It delves into his vulnerability. It’s a moment of quietude in the face of the all-consuming greed that drives the narrative. The scene is a perfect demonstration of Leone's mastery of character development. The confrontation between the brothers, the accusations, the longing for redemption, is never openly explained nor justified. The questions it raises are far more important than any answers. It reveals Tuco's humanity, not merely his criminality. To me, it highlights that even in the brutal world of the Wild West, men are still men.
